questions.title: INNER JOIN vs. LEFT JOIN
questions.prompt: In SQL Server, what is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN? Specifically, what happens to rows that don't have a match on the other side in each case?
questions.modelAnswer: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the ON condition evaluates true on both sides — any row from either table that has no match on the other side is dropped from the result entirely. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in the FROM clause (the 'left' table), whether or not it has a match in the table named after JOIN (the 'right' table). When a left-table row has no match, every column that would have come from the right table comes back as NULL instead of the row being dropped. 'Left' and 'right' describe position in the query text — the table in FROM is left, the table after JOIN is right — not anything about the size or importance of the data. A common real use of LEFT JOIN is combining it with WHERE <right-table-column> IS NULL to find rows that have no match at all, since that column can only be NULL if the join failed to find a partner row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with a concrete example: if I join Product to SalesOrderDetail with an INNER JOIN, I only see products that have actually sold — a product sitting in inventory with zero orders just disappears from the result, because there's nothing on the right side to pair it with. If my actual question is 'show me every product, including the ones that have never sold,' INNER JOIN can't answer that by definition, so I switch to a LEFT JOIN from Product. Now every product shows up, and for the ones with no matching order, the order columns just come back NULL. That NULL is actually useful — if I add WHERE OrderQty IS NULL to that LEFT JOIN, I've just built a 'products that have never sold' report, which is a query I get asked for constantly in a reporting role. The one thing I'm careful to remember is that left and right only refer to where I physically wrote the table in the query, not which table is 'bigger' or more important.
questions.example:
-- INNER JOIN: only products with at least one order line
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- LEFT JOIN: every product, NULL-filled when there's no match
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- Finding products that have NEVER sold
SELECT p.Name
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID
WHERE sod.ProductID IS NULL;
commonMistakes: Thinking 'left' and 'right' describe which table has more rows or matters more, instead of just position in the FROM/JOIN clause
Forgetting that unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL, then getting confused when COUNT() or SUM() on those columns behaves unexpectedly
Using INNER JOIN when the real goal is to find rows with no match — that specifically requires LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL check
Not realizing WHERE runs after the join, so a WHERE clause on a right-side column can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN back into something that behaves like an INNER JOIN
keyPoints: INNER JOIN returns only rows matching on both sides
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in FROM, matched or not
Left/right refer to position in the query, not data meaning or size
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL in a LEFT JOIN
LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is the standard pattern for finding unmatched rows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what each join type returns
Explains NULL behavior for unmatched LEFT JOIN rows
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: WHERE vs. HAVING
questions.prompt: Why can't you filter on the result of an aggregate function (like AVG or COUNT) using a WHERE clause, and how does HAVING solve that problem? What is the correct logical order of FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, and ORDER BY?
questions.modelAnswer: WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY runs, so at the point WHERE executes, groups and their aggregated values (like AVG(ListPrice)) don't exist yet — there's nothing for WHERE to compare against. HAVING is WHERE's counterpart for groups: it runs after GROUP BY has formed the groups and after the aggregate functions have been computed, so by the time HAVING evaluates, every group's aggregate already exists and can be filtered on. The correct logical processing order in T-SQL is: FROM (and JOIN) first, then WHERE filters individual rows, then GROUP BY forms groups, then HAVING filters those groups, then SELECT picks the columns/expressions to return, and finally ORDER BY sorts the final result. WHERE and HAVING aren't mutually exclusive — you commonly use WHERE to remove rows before grouping even starts, and HAVING to filter the groups that result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as a timeline problem, not a syntax problem. If I write WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500, SQL Server throws an error, because logically WHERE runs before GROUP BY has even created any groups — there's no average to check yet. The moment I actually need to filter on an aggregated value, I move that condition to HAVING, which runs after the grouping and aggregation have already happened. In practice I use both together constantly: WHERE Color IS NOT NULL to throw out rows with no color recorded before I even start grouping, then GROUP BY Color, then HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500 to keep only the color groups whose average price clears that bar. I always come back to the same six-step order — FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY — whenever I'm unsure why a query is or isn't behaving the way I expect.
questions.example:
SELECT Color, AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500;
-- WHERE removes NULL-color rows before grouping; HAVING keeps only
-- the color groups whose computed average price exceeds 500.
commonMistakes: Writing WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500 and being surprised by the error instead of recognizing aggregates aren't available yet at that stage
Assuming WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable, rather than realizing WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups
Not knowing the logical processing order, which makes debugging any non-trivial query much harder
Putting a filter that doesn't need aggregation into HAVING instead of WHERE, which is valid but wastes work filtering rows that could have been removed earlier
keyPoints: WHERE filters individual rows and runs before GROUP BY
HAVING filters groups and runs after GROUP BY and aggregation
Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY
WHERE and HAVING can and often should be used together

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why WHERE can't reference aggregates
Correctly states the logical processing order
Explains how WHERE and HAVING work together

questions.title: Primary keys vs. foreign keys
questions.prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY constraint guarantee about a column, and what does a FOREIGN KEY constraint enforce between two tables? What happens if you try to insert a row that violates a foreign key?
questions.modelAnswer: A primary key guarantees two things at once about a column (or set of columns): every value is unique, and no value is ever NULL — together that means a primary key value always identifies exactly one row. Creating a primary key without specifying otherwise also builds a clustered index on it by default, physically sorting the table by that key. A foreign key enforces referential integrity: every value in the foreign-key column must already exist as a primary-key value in the referenced table. Trying to insert or update a row with a foreign-key value that doesn't exist in the referenced table fails with error 547 — the database physically refuses to create the orphaned row. ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default behavior (which blocks deleting a referenced row while dependents still point to it) so that deleting a parent row automatically deletes its dependent rows too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the primary key as the table's identity guarantee — Production.Product's primary key, ProductID, means I can always find exactly one product for a given ID, never zero, never two. The foreign key is what makes a JOIN trustworthy: Product.ProductSubcategoryID is a foreign key to ProductSubcategory, so SQL Server physically won't let me insert a product pointing at a subcategory that doesn't exist. If I try, I get error 547, which is the database doing its job, not a bug to work around. I'm careful with ON DELETE CASCADE, though — it's convenient for cleaning up dependent rows automatically, but on a deep relationship chain it can silently delete far more data than I expect, so I think through the blast radius before turning it on.
commonMistakes: Thinking a primary key only guarantees uniqueness and forgetting it also guarantees NOT NULL
Not realizing a primary key builds a clustered index by default unless you explicitly say NONCLUSTERED
Assuming a foreign key violation is just a warning rather than a hard failure (error 547) that blocks the write
Adding ON DELETE CASCADE without considering how far the deletion could cascade through a longer relationship chain
keyPoints: Primary key = unique + NOT NULL, identifying exactly one row
Primary key creates a clustered index by default
Foreign key enforces that a value must exist as a primary key in another table
Violating a foreign key raises Error 547
ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default block-on-delete behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a primary key guarantees
Correctly describes referential integrity and Error 547
Mentions the clustered index / cascade nuance

questions.title: CTEs vs. regular subqueries
questions.prompt: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE), and how does it differ from writing the same logic as a regular subquery? Why might you prefer a CTE?
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named, temporary result set defined at the top of a query with the WITH keyword. Functionally, it's equivalent to putting the same SELECT inside a subquery in the FROM clause — but instead of nesting it inline, you give it a name once and then reference that name like a real table in the statement that follows. This makes deeply nested subqueries much easier to read, especially when the same intermediate result needs to be referenced more than once in the outer query. A CTE is strictly temporary: it only exists for the single statement immediately following its WITH clause, is never saved anywhere, and disappears the moment that statement finishes — unlike a VIEW, which is a genuinely reusable, saved named query.
questions.professionalAnswer: I reach for a CTE mainly for readability. A subquery nested three levels deep inside a FROM clause gets hard to read fast — you end up mentally tracking which closing parenthesis belongs to which level. If I give that same logic a name with WITH CategoryAverages AS (...), I can read the outer query almost like English: 'from CategoryAverages, where...' That's especially valuable when I need to reference the same intermediate calculation more than once in the final query, since a CTE lets me do that without repeating the underlying SELECT. The one thing I always clarify for someone newer to this is that a CTE isn't a saved object — it only lives for the one statement right after it, so if I need that same logic reused across multiple separate queries, a VIEW is the right tool, not a CTE.
questions.example:
WITH CategoryAverages AS (
    SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID
)
SELECT ca1.ProductSubcategoryID, ca1.AvgPrice
FROM CategoryAverages AS ca1
WHERE ca1.AvgPrice > (SELECT AVG(AvgPrice) FROM CategoryAverages);
-- CategoryAverages is referenced twice in one statement -- hard to
-- do cleanly with a nested subquery instead.
commonMistakes: Thinking a CTE is saved/reusable across separate queries like a VIEW, rather than scoped to one statement
Not taking advantage of referencing the same CTE multiple times in the outer query
Assuming a CTE is always faster than a subquery -- it's primarily a readability tool, not automatically a performance one
Forgetting the WITH keyword needs to be the first word of the batch (or preceded by a semicolon) in some contexts
keyPoints: CTE = a named, temporary result set defined with WITH
Functionally equivalent to a FROM-clause subquery, but far more readable
Can be referenced multiple times in the statement that follows it
Scoped to one statement only -- not saved like a VIEW

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what a CTE is
Explains the readability/multiple-reference advantage
Correctly notes the CTE is scoped to one statement, unlike a VIEW

questions.title: Measures vs. calculated columns in Power BI
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a calculated column and a measure in Power BI, and what's a simple rule for deciding which one you need for a given situation?
questions.modelAnswer: A calculated column is computed once, when data is entered or refreshed, and stored per row in row context -- it adds to the model's size and updates only when the table refreshes. A measure is computed dynamically every time it's viewed, evaluated in filter context (whatever's currently filtering the report), and isn't stored at all -- it recalculates instantly as filters change. The decision rule is: do you need to slice, filter, or group by this value, or just display a summarized number? If you need a new category to filter, group, or put in a slicer/legend/axis, you need a calculated column, because only columns are filterable. If you need a calculated number that summarizes -- a total, average, ratio, or projection -- you need a measure. Choosing wrong doesn't throw an error: a calculated column used where a measure was needed freezes at refresh-time values and goes silently stale as filters change; a measure used where a column was needed simply can't be dragged into a slicer or axis at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give the one-question test I actually use: am I going to filter or group by this, or am I just going to display a summarized number? A customer loyalty tier based on total purchases is something I'd want in a slicer, so that's a calculated column. Total revenue that should recalculate as someone clicks through a report is a measure. The part I'd specifically warn a newer analyst about is that getting this wrong doesn't throw an error -- it just quietly produces the wrong behavior. A calculated column written where a measure belonged freezes at whatever it computed during the last refresh and goes stale the moment someone applies a filter; a measure written where a column belonged simply won't let you drag it into a slicer at all, since measures aren't filterable, only summarizable.
questions.example:
CityState = [City] & "," & [State]                              -- calculated column: used to group/display
Projected Sales = SUM('Reseller Sales'[Last Years Sales]) * 1.06  -- measure: dynamic, filter-context aware
commonMistakes: Writing a calculated column when a dynamically-recalculating measure was actually needed
Trying to drag a measure into a slicer or axis and not understanding why it isn't allowed
Not realizing calculated columns add to model size on every row, while measures add none
Assuming a wrong choice will throw an obvious error instead of silently producing stale or unusable results
keyPoints: Calculated column: computed once per row, stored, row context, filterable
Measure: computed dynamically, not stored, filter context, summarizable only
Decision rule: filter/group by it -> column; summarize/display it -> measure
Getting it wrong doesn't error -- it silently misbehaves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes storage/evaluation differences
States a clear, usable decision rule
Explains the silent-failure consequence of choosing wrong

questions.title: Import vs. DirectQuery
questions.prompt: What's the core trade-off between Import and DirectQuery storage modes in Power BI, and why can you convert a DirectQuery table to Import but never the other way around?
questions.modelAnswer: Import copies the data into the Power BI file: visuals read from memory, so they're fast, and the model has full DAX feature support, but the data is only as fresh as the last refresh and is limited by file size (roughly a 1 GB typical cap). DirectQuery leaves the data in the source and queries it live every time a visual loads: it handles very large sources and gives truly real-time data, but visual speed depends entirely on the source's own speed, and some DAX/modeling features are restricted. Import is the default choice for most real reports and for learning, because of full feature support and no dependency on a live connection while working; DirectQuery earns its place when the source is too large to import practically, the data must be truly real-time, or a security policy requires data to never leave its source system. You can convert a DirectQuery table to Import because that's simply choosing to copy and cache data that was already being queried live -- but going the other direction would mean somehow 'un-caching' data and re-establishing a live query path, which isn't a simple reversal, so Power BI doesn't support converting Import back to DirectQuery.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as a speed-versus-freshness-versus-scale trade-off. Import is fast because everything's sitting in memory, and it gets full DAX support with no dependency on the source being reachable while I work -- that's why it's the default for basically every lesson and most real reports. DirectQuery trades that speed for currency and scale: the data never leaves the source, so it's always live, and there's no 1 GB-ish file-size ceiling, but now every visual's performance is only as good as the source database's performance, and some features aren't available. The one-way-door detail I'd flag explicitly: you can always switch a DirectQuery table to Import, since that's just deciding to start caching data you were already querying live, but you can't go back -- there's no clean way to 'un-cache' Import data and reconnect it as a live query, so if I'm unsure which mode I'll end up needing, I start with DirectQuery and convert later rather than the reverse.
commonMistakes: Assuming DirectQuery is always 'better' because it's real-time, ignoring the source-dependent performance cost
Not knowing Import has a practical file-size ceiling (around 1 GB)
Forgetting some DAX/modeling features are restricted under DirectQuery
Not realizing the Import conversion is one-directional -- DirectQuery to Import only, never back
keyPoints: Import: data copied into the file, fast, full feature support, refresh-dependent freshness
DirectQuery: data stays in source, live, scales to large sources, source-dependent speed
Import is the default for most reports; DirectQuery fits huge/real-time/security-constrained sources
You can convert DirectQuery to Import, never the reverse

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the Import vs. DirectQuery trade-off
Correctly explains the one-directional conversion
Gives a sensible real scenario for choosing DirectQuery

questions.title: UNION vs. UNION ALL
questions.prompt: In T-SQL, what's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL when combining the result sets of two SELECT statements, and what two conditions must both SELECT statements satisfy before you can combine them at all?
questions.modelAnswer: UNION combines the rows returned by two (or more) SELECT statements into one result set and removes any duplicate rows from that combined set, which requires SQL Server to do an implicit sort/distinct pass over the whole combined output. UNION ALL also combines the rows, but keeps every row exactly as returned, duplicates included, and skips the dedup pass entirely -- which makes it faster and cheaper to run whenever duplicates either can't occur or genuinely don't matter. Both statements being combined must return the same number of columns, and the data type in each corresponding column position must be compatible (not necessarily identical, but implicitly convertible) -- column names in the final result come from the first SELECT statement, regardless of what the second one used.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default to UNION ALL unless I actually have a reason to expect duplicates and need them removed, because UNION ALL skips the sort/distinct work UNION does under the hood, so it's just cheaper to run on anything beyond a trivial row count. The two things I always check before combining two SELECTs this way: same number of columns on both sides, and compatible data types lining up column-by-column -- if the second SELECT's third column is a different, incompatible type from the first's third column, the combine fails outright. One detail that trips people up is that the final column names come entirely from the first SELECT -- aliasing a column differently in the second query doesn't change anything in the output.
questions.example:
-- UNION: removes duplicate rows across both queries
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';

-- UNION ALL: keeps every row, including duplicates, and skips the dedup work
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION ALL
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';
commonMistakes: Using UNION by default everywhere, paying for a dedup pass that isn't actually needed
Assuming the two SELECTs need identical column names instead of just a matching column count and compatible types
Not realizing the final result's column names come from the first SELECT, regardless of aliases used in the second
Forgetting ORDER BY can only appear once, at the very end of the combined statement, not after each individual SELECT
keyPoints: UNION removes duplicate rows across the combined result sets; UNION ALL keeps every row
UNION ALL is cheaper -- it skips the sort/distinct pass UNION performs
Both SELECTs must return the same number of columns with compatible data types per position
Result column names come from the first SELECT statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the duplicate-removal difference
Correctly states the column-count/data-type compatibility requirement
Mentions the performance implication of the dedup pass

questions.title: Dimensions vs. Measures in Tableau
questions.prompt: In Tableau, what's the difference between a Dimension and a Measure, and how does the discrete/continuous distinction (blue vs. green pills) layer on top of that? Why does it matter which one you drag onto Rows or Columns?
questions.modelAnswer: Dimensions are qualitative, categorical fields -- Tableau treats them as discrete (blue pill) by default: Region, Product Category, Customer Name -- values used to slice, group, or label data, where each distinct value becomes its own header or mark. Measures are quantitative, numeric fields that can be aggregated -- Tableau treats them as continuous (green pill) by default: Sales, Profit, Quantity -- plotted along an axis rather than listed as headers. The discrete/continuous distinction is actually independent of dimension/measure in Tableau: any pill can be switched (right-click -> Convert to Discrete/Continuous), but the practical default pairing (dimension = discrete = blue, measure = continuous = green) is what drives whether something becomes a header (discrete) or an axis (continuous). Dragging a discrete field onto Columns creates separate headers, one per distinct value; dragging a continuous field onto Columns creates a single continuous axis. Mixing this up -- for instance making Year discrete instead of continuous -- changes a line chart into a series of disconnected per-year columns instead of one continuous trend line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the blue/green color-coding since that's literally how Tableau shows it on the Data pane. Blue pills are discrete -- categorical things like Region or Category -- and when I drag one onto Columns, I get one separate header per distinct value. Green pills are continuous -- numeric things like Sales -- and dragging one onto an axis gives me a single continuous scale instead of a list of headers. The part that trips people up is that Year, which looks like it should always be a measure because it's a number, is actually a date dimension, and whether I want it discrete or continuous changes the chart completely: continuous Year draws one connected trend line, while discrete Year draws a separate bar or column per year with no line connecting them. So before I build a chart, I'm deliberately checking both things -- is this a dimension or a measure, and do I want it discrete or continuous -- because they're two separate decisions, not one.
commonMistakes: Assuming discrete/continuous is just another name for dimension/measure instead of a separate, switchable setting
Making a date field discrete when a continuous trend line was actually wanted, or vice versa
Not noticing the blue/green pill color as the visual cue for discrete vs. continuous
Expecting a measure to work as a row/column header the same way a dimension does
keyPoints: Dimensions: categorical, default discrete (blue), create headers
Measures: numeric/aggregatable, default continuous (green), create axes
Discrete vs. continuous is a separate, switchable setting from dimension vs. measure
Continuous fields draw a single axis/line; discrete fields draw separate headers per value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes dimensions from measures
Correctly explains discrete vs. continuous as independent of that
Gives a concrete example of how the choice changes a chart

questions.title: VLOOKUP vs. XLOOKUP
questions.prompt: What are the main limitations of VLOOKUP that XLOOKUP was built to fix, and why would you recommend a data analyst use XLOOKUP by default going forward?
questions.modelAnswer: VLOOKUP searches only the leftmost column of a specified range and always returns a value from a column to its right, counted by a positional index number -- meaning the lookup column must physically be the first column in the range, and inserting or deleting a column shifts that index number and silently breaks the formula. VLOOKUP's approximate-match behavior also defaults to TRUE (approximate) unless you explicitly type FALSE, a default that quietly returns a plausible-looking wrong answer when an exact match doesn't exist. XLOOKUP removes the left-to-right restriction entirely -- the lookup array and return array are specified as two separate ranges, so the return column can sit anywhere, including to the left of the lookup column. XLOOKUP also defaults to exact match (not approximate), has a built-in if-not-found argument so a missing value doesn't need a separate IFERROR wrapper, and can search in reverse order. The practical recommendation is to default to XLOOKUP for new work: it's harder to misuse by default, self-documents its own missing-value behavior, and doesn't break silently when a column is inserted elsewhere in the sheet.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd list the two VLOOKUP gotchas I've actually been burned by. First, VLOOKUP only looks right -- the column I want back has to be to the right of the column I'm searching, which means if someone inserts a new column into the source data later, that hard-coded index number now points at the wrong column and the formula just returns something different with no error at all. Second, VLOOKUP's match type defaults to approximate unless I remember to type FALSE, so a typo in a lookup value can still return a plausible but wrong answer instead of an error. XLOOKUP fixes both: I give it a lookup array and a separate return array, so direction doesn't matter at all, and it defaults to exact match, so a genuine mismatch shows clearly instead of pretending to work. It also has a built-in 'if not found' argument, so I don't need to wrap it in IFERROR just to handle a missing value. At this point I default to XLOOKUP for anything new and only reach for VLOOKUP when I'm stuck on an older Excel version that doesn't have it.
questions.example:
=XLOOKUP(A2, Prices[ProductID], Prices[UnitPrice], "Not found")
-- Compare to the older equivalent:
=VLOOKUP(A2, Prices!A:C, 3, FALSE)
-- VLOOKUP's "3" breaks silently if a column is ever inserted into A:C.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to type FALSE in VLOOKUP and getting a silently wrong approximate match
Hard-coding a VLOOKUP column index that breaks the moment someone inserts a column
Wrapping XLOOKUP in IFERROR out of habit instead of using its built-in if-not-found argument
Assuming VLOOKUP can look to its left, instead of needing INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP for that
keyPoints: VLOOKUP only returns values to the right of the lookup column, via a positional index that breaks when columns shift
VLOOKUP defaults to approximate match unless FALSE is specified
XLOOKUP uses separate lookup/return arrays, so direction doesn't matter
XLOOKUP defaults to exact match and has a built-in if-not-found argument

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies VLOOKUP's directional/index limitation
Correctly identifies the approximate-match default risk
Explains why XLOOKUP resolves both

questions.title: What a pandas DataFrame actually is
questions.prompt: What is a pandas DataFrame, and why does a Power BI-focused analyst benefit from learning a little Python/pandas on top of Power Query and DAX?
questions.modelAnswer: A pandas DataFrame is a two-dimensional, labeled data structure -- rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or a SQL result set -- that lives in memory while a Python script runs, built on top of the pandas library. Each column has its own data type, every row has a label (an index, by default just 0, 1, 2...), and the structure is well-suited for exactly the kind of row-and-column data analysts already work with in Excel and Power Query. The value for a Power BI-focused analyst isn't that Python replaces Power Query or DAX -- it's that Python/pandas fills a gap when a transformation is genuinely hard or impossible to express cleanly in either: complex text cleaning with regular expressions, statistical operations Power Query doesn't offer, or pulling in a specialized Python library for something like fuzzy matching or a calculation Power Query's UI simply has no step for. It also matters because a Python script can run as a step inside Power Query itself (Transform Data using Python) or power a custom Python visual directly in a report, so it isn't an entirely separate tool so much as an occasional extra option alongside the two an analyst already knows.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a DataFrame as basically a spreadsheet that lives inside a running Python script instead of inside Excel -- rows, columns, each column with its own type, and an index labeling every row. I wouldn't tell someone to go learn Python because Power Query and DAX are somehow lacking -- for the vast majority of real transformations, they're the right tool and I'd use them first. Where Python earns its place is the occasional transformation that's awkward in either: cleaning messy text with a regular expression, or pulling in a statistical function that Power Query's UI just doesn't expose a step for. The part that makes it worth learning rather than treating as a separate skill entirely is that it plugs directly into the tools I already use -- I can run a Python script as a transform step right inside Power Query, or build a custom Python visual inside a Power BI report -- so it's one more tool in the same toolbox, not a different toolbox altogether.
commonMistakes: Thinking a DataFrame is fundamentally different from a spreadsheet instead of a very similar row/column structure in memory
Assuming learning Python means replacing Power Query and DAX instead of supplementing them for specific gaps
Not realizing Python can run as a step inside Power Query itself, not just as a completely separate process
Reaching for Python by default instead of trying Power Query/DAX first for a transformation they already handle well
keyPoints: A DataFrame is a two-dimensional, labeled, in-memory row/column structure, similar to a spreadsheet
Python/pandas supplements Power Query and DAX, it doesn't replace them
Python fills gaps like complex text cleaning, regex, or statistical operations the other tools don't offer
Python can run inside Power Query (Transform Data using Python) or power a custom visual

Correctly frames Python as supplementing, not replacing, Power Query/DAX

questions.title: Write a GROUP BY aggregate query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns each distinct Color along with the count of products of that color and the average ListPrice for that color, excluding rows where Color is NULL.
questions.code:
-- Production.Product (AdventureWorks2012) has columns including:
-- ProductID, Name, Color, ListPrice
USE AdventureWorks2012;
GO
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY works in three conceptual steps: split the table into groups (one group per distinct Color value), aggregate within each group separately (COUNT and AVG each run once per group, not once overall), then combine the results into one row per group. Every column in SELECT must either be wrapped in an aggregate function or listed in GROUP BY — Color qualifies because it's the GROUP BY column; Name would not be allowed unaggregated here because it varies within a color group. Filtering out NULL colors belongs in WHERE, since that's a row-level filter that should happen before grouping, not a group-level filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write WHERE Color IS NOT NULL first, since that's just removing rows before grouping even starts — no reason to let NULL colors form their own group if the business doesn't care about them. Then GROUP BY Color splits the remaining rows into one bucket per color, and COUNT(*) plus AVG(ListPrice) each compute their own answer per bucket rather than one answer for the whole table. The result has exactly one row per distinct color — the same number of rows COUNT(DISTINCT Color) would report — which is a good sanity check I'd run after writing a query like this.
questions.example:
SELECT Color,
       COUNT(*) AS ProductCount,
       AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
ORDER BY ProductCount DESC;
-- One row per distinct Color; COUNT and AVG are computed per color group.
commonMistakes: Adding Name or another non-aggregated, non-grouped column to SELECT and getting a GROUP BY error
Filtering NULL colors with HAVING instead of WHERE, doing unnecessary work by grouping rows that should have been excluded first

questions.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK side by side
questions.prompt: Write a query that ranks products by ListPrice descending using ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in the same result set, and explain how the three functions differ when two products are tied for the same price.
questions.modelAnswer: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique, sequential numbers — even for genuinely tied values, it arbitrarily breaks the tie and gives one row a lower number than the other. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but leaves a gap afterward: if two products tie for rank 1, the next distinct price gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() accounts for how many rows were tied at the previous rank. DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but with no gap — the next distinct price after a tie at rank 1 gets rank 2. All three are computed with an OVER (ORDER BY ...) window clause and require no GROUP BY.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run all three in one query so the difference is visible directly in the output rather than just described. If two products are tied for the most expensive, ROW_NUMBER() pretends there's no tie at all and numbers them 1 and 2 arbitrarily — which would misrepresent a genuine tie as a win. RANK() is honest about the tie: both get rank 1, but the next product jumps to rank 3, because two rows already occupied rank 1's 'slot.' DENSE_RANK() is also honest about the tie — both get rank 1 — but it only cares about distinct values, so the next price tier is rank 2 with no gap. Which one I pick depends on the business question: a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for second place genuinely skips third place calls for RANK(); a scale of distinct price tiers where I just want the next gap-free tier number calls for DENSE_RANK().
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- Tied prices: RowNum stays unique, Rank_ ties then skips ahead,
-- DenseRank_ ties with no gap.
commonMistakes: Assuming ROW_NUMBER() is 'safer' for ties when it actually hides them by assigning arbitrary unique numbers
Confusing RANK's gap-after-a-tie behavior with DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Forgetting that ORDER BY inside OVER() determines which rows get which rank — changing it changes the whole result
Trying to use these functions without an OVER() clause, or expecting them to need a GROUP BY
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, even for ties
RANK() ties share a number but the next value skips ahead by the tie size
DENSE_RANK() ties share a number with no gap for the next distinct value
All three run inside OVER (ORDER BY ...), no GROUP BY needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct syntax for all three ranking functions
Accurately explains the tie-handling difference
Picks a sensible real-world scenario for each function

questions.title: Write a parameterized stored procedure
questions.prompt: Write a stored procedure named usp_GetProductsAbovePrice that accepts a @MinPrice parameter defaulting to 100, and returns the Name and ListPrice of every product in Production.Product with a ListPrice at or above that value, ordered by price descending. Then show how you'd call it both with and without supplying a value for @MinPrice.
questions.modelAnswer: A parameter is declared right after the procedure name, before the AS keyword, and behaves like a normal variable throughout the procedure body — it's just pre-populated from whatever the caller passes in. Giving a parameter a default value (@MinPrice MONEY = 100) makes it optional: if the caller doesn't supply a value, SQL Server uses the default automatically. Calling the procedure with named notation (EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500) is unambiguous and order-independent, which is why it's preferred over positional calling once a procedure has more than one parameter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the parameter with a sensible default so the procedure is usable both ways out of the box. The body itself is just the same filtered, sorted SELECT I'd write ad hoc, except @MinPrice stands in for whatever literal value I'd otherwise hard-code. Calling it with EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice; uses the default of 100 automatically, and calling it with @MinPrice = 500 overrides that for just this call. I always call with named parameters -- @MinPrice = 500 instead of just 500 -- because the moment a procedure picks up a second or third parameter, positional calling becomes an easy way to silently pass values to the wrong parameter.
questions.example:
CREATE PROCEDURE usp_GetProductsAbovePrice
    @MinPrice MONEY = 100
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT Name, ListPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    WHERE ListPrice >= @MinPrice
    ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
END;
GO

EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500; -- overrides the default
EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice;                 -- uses the default, 100
commonMistakes: Forgetting the default value, which forces every caller to always supply @MinPrice even when a sensible default exists
Calling the procedure positionally once it has multiple parameters, risking values landing in the wrong parameter
Putting the parameter declaration after AS instead of before it
Hard-coding the price threshold inside the procedure body instead of parameterizing it, defeating the point of a reusable procedure
keyPoints: Parameters are declared before AS and behave like pre-populated variables
A default value makes a parameter optional
Named notation (@Param = value) is unambiguous and order-independent
EXEC without a value for an optional parameter falls back to its default

questions.title: Write a CALCULATE-based DAX measure
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure called 'Blue Revenue' that sums SalesAmount from a Sales table, but only for rows where the related Product table's Color column equals 'Blue'. Then explain what happens to that measure's result if the report already has a slicer filtering Product[Color] to 'Red' when 'Blue Revenue' is displayed.
questions.code: -- Model: Sales[SalesAmount], 'Product'[Color], related by a relationship
questions.modelAnswer: CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside a modified filter context: CALCULATE(<expression>, <filter1>, <filter2>, ...). Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue") sums SalesAmount but only for rows where Product[Color] equals 'Blue'. When a filter argument targets a column that's already filtered elsewhere in the report (like a slicer set to 'Red'), CALCULATE's filter overwrites the existing one for that expression rather than combining with it -- so Blue Revenue still shows blue-only totals even with the Red slicer active, because CALCULATE's explicit filter on Color replaces whatever the slicer was doing to that same column.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue"). The part I'd specifically call out in an interview is the overwrite behavior: if a report already has a slicer set to Color = 'Red', my Blue Revenue measure doesn't get combined with that -- it overwrites it for this expression, because CALCULATE's filter argument always wins over an existing filter on the same column. So no matter what the user has selected in that slicer, Blue Revenue keeps showing blue-only totals, which is exactly the point: CALCULATE lets me force a measure to ignore what the user selected and substitute my own condition instead.
questions.example:
Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue")
-- Even with a report-level slicer set to Color = "Red", this measure
-- still returns blue-only totals, because CALCULATE's filter argument
-- overwrites the existing filter on the same column for this expression.
commonMistakes: Writing SUMX or FILTER where a simple CALCULATE + Boolean filter argument would be clearer and sufficient
Assuming CALCULATE's filter combines (ANDs) with an existing slicer on the same column instead of overwriting it
Forgetting the expression argument (SUM(...)) is what's actually being calculated -- the rest are just filter conditions
Quoting the table name incorrectly when the table name contains a space (needs 'Product' with quotes if there's a space, e.g. 'Reseller Sales')
keyPoints: CALCULATE(<expression>, <filter1>, ...) evaluates an expression in a modified filter context
A filter argument on an already-filtered column overwrites that filter for this expression
This overwrite behavior is what makes CALCULATE able to ignore user selections deliberately
KEEPFILTERS exists specifically to change this default overwrite behavior when needed

Correctly explains the overwrite behavior against the Red slicer
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Creating a static RLS role
questions.prompt: Describe the steps to create a static row-level security (RLS) role in Power BI Desktop named 'West Sales' that restricts a report to only show rows where Region equals 'West.' Why can't you finish testing or assigning users to this role entirely inside Desktop?
questions.modelAnswer: In Desktop, go to the Modeling tab and select Manage Roles, then New. Name the role 'West Sales' (commas aren't allowed in role names). Under Select tables, pick the table holding the Region column -- for example DimSalesTerritory. Under Filter data, use the default drop-down editor (since this is a simple static filter, not one needing a DAX function like USERPRINCIPALNAME()) and set the filter to [Region] = "West". Save, then publish the semantic model. Every DAX filter expression returns TRUE or FALSE per row, and only rows evaluating TRUE stay visible, so anyone later assigned to this role sees only rows where Region equals 'West.' You cannot assign users to the role from inside Desktop at all -- that step, along with fully testing the role as a specific user would see it, only exists once the semantic model is published to the Power BI service.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it exactly as Desktop presents it: Modeling tab, Manage Roles, New, name it West Sales, pick the table that actually has the Region column -- DimSalesTerritory in an AdventureWorksDW2014-style model -- and since this is a plain static filter, the default drop-down editor is enough; I'd set it to [Region] = "West" rather than switching to the DAX editor, which I'd only need for something dynamic like USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Save, publish, done -- as far as Desktop is concerned. The thing I'd flag clearly is that creating the role and assigning a person to it are two completely separate steps in two completely separate places: Desktop only lets me define the rule, and assigning an actual user to 'West Sales' only happens once the model is in the Power BI service, so I can't fully test what a specific user would see until it's published.

Switching to the DAX editor unnecessarily for a simple static filter that the default editor already handles
Using a comma in the role name, which isn't allowed
Forgetting to publish the semantic model before assuming the role is usable anywhere

Default editor handles static filters; DAX editor is needed only for dynamic ones (USERPRINCIPALNAME, etc.)
Every filter expression returns TRUE/FALSE per row; only TRUE rows stay visible
User assignment happens only in the Power BI service, never in Desktop

questions.title: Create a Profit Ratio calculated field
questions.prompt: Write a Tableau calculated field named 'Profit Ratio' that divides total Profit by total Sales, and explain why it needs to be written with SUM() around each field rather than just Profit / Sales.
questions.modelAnswer: The calculated field should be written as SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]). Writing it as plain [Profit] / [Sales] would divide row by row before any aggregation happens, producing a ratio per individual transaction row rather than the business's actual profit margin -- and because Tableau aggregates calculated fields for display, an un-aggregated ratio written that way gets summed or averaged afterward in a way that doesn't equal the true overall ratio (averaging a set of per-row ratios is not mathematically the same as dividing the total profit by the total sales). Wrapping each field in SUM() forces the aggregation to happen first -- total profit across every row in the current view, divided by total sales across every row in the current view -- which gives the one correct ratio that actually matches how profit margin is normally reported.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it as SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]), and the SUM() around each piece isn't optional styling -- it changes what's actually being calculated. Without it, Tableau computes Profit / Sales once per row, before anything is totaled, which gives me a profit ratio for one single transaction, not the category or region I'm actually looking at. If I then let Tableau aggregate that per-row ratio (say, by averaging it across all the rows in a bar), I get the average of a bunch of individual ratios, which is a different number from the true overall margin -- dividing total profit by total sales. Wrapping both fields in SUM() forces the totals to be computed first, so the division happens on the totals, which is the number that actually matches how a profit margin is reported in any real business context.
questions.example:
Profit Ratio = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])
-- WRONG: [Profit] / [Sales] computes a row-level ratio before
-- aggregation, which is not the same as the overall margin.

questions.title: Write an XLOOKUP formula with a fallback value
questions.prompt: You have a Prices sheet with a ProductID lookup table (columns ProductID, UnitPrice), and an Orders sheet where column A has a ProductID that needs its UnitPrice pulled in. Write an XLOOKUP formula for cell B2 of Orders that returns the matching UnitPrice, and shows the text 'Price not found' instead of an error if a ProductID doesn't exist in Prices.
questions.code:
-- Orders!A2 = ProductID to look up
-- Prices!A:B = ProductID, UnitPrice
questions.modelAnswer: =XLOOKUP(A2, Prices!A:A, Prices!B:B, "Price not found") -- the first argument is the lookup value, the second is the range to search, the third is the range to pull the result from (which can be anywhere relative to the lookup range, not necessarily to its right), and the fourth, optional argument is what to return if no match is found, which XLOOKUP handles natively without needing a separate IFERROR wrapper around the whole formula. This is cleaner than the older VLOOKUP-plus-IFERROR pattern (=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(A2,Prices!A:B,2,FALSE),"Price not found")) because XLOOKUP's fourth argument only catches a genuine no-match case, while a blanket IFERROR wrapper would also silently swallow a real formula error -- like a typo in a sheet name -- and still show 'Price not found,' masking a completely different kind of problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write =XLOOKUP(A2, Prices!A:A, Prices!B:B, "Price not found"). The fourth argument is XLOOKUP's built-in if-not-found behavior, so I don't need to wrap the whole thing in IFERROR the way I would have had to with VLOOKUP. That distinction actually matters beyond just being shorter to type -- a blanket IFERROR around a VLOOKUP would hide a genuine formula error, like a mistyped sheet name, behind the same 'Price not found' message as an honest missing value, which makes a real bug much harder to spot. XLOOKUP's fourth argument only fires for an actual no-match, so if something else breaks in the formula, I'd still see Excel's normal error instead of a message that quietly lies about what went wrong.

questions.title: Debugging a WHERE = NULL mistake
questions.prompt: A junior developer writes WHERE MiddleName = NULL to find customers with no middle name recorded, and gets zero rows back — even though many customers genuinely have a NULL MiddleName. What's actually wrong with that query, and how should they fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents an unknown or not-applicable value, not zero or an empty string. Because it's unknown, NULL can't be said to equal anything — not even another NULL — so any comparison using the = operator against NULL evaluates to unknown (treated as false), never true. That means WHERE MiddleName = NULL will always return zero rows, regardless of how many rows actually have a NULL MiddleName, because the comparison can never succeed. The fix is to use the special IS NULL syntax instead: WHERE MiddleName IS NULL. IS NULL isn't a comparison operator — it's dedicated syntax built specifically to test for the absence of a value, and it works correctly where = cannot. The same logic applies to IS NOT NULL for the opposite case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out is that this isn't a typo or syntax error — the query runs fine, it just silently returns the wrong answer, which is the dangerous kind of bug. I'd explain that NULL means 'unknown,' and you can't compare an unknown value to anything using = and expect a meaningful true or false — SQL Server treats that comparison as unknown, which gets filtered out just like false. So WHERE MiddleName = NULL isn't matching NULLs, it's failing to match anything at all. The fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, which is purpose-built syntax for exactly this case rather than a regular comparison. If the goal were actually to display something readable instead of filtering, I'd reach for ISNULL(MiddleName, '(none)') or COALESCE for more than two fallback values.

Treating NULL as if it were an empty string or zero instead of 'unknown'
Using = NULL or <> NULL anywhere instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Confusing ISNULL() (replaces a NULL with a default, two arguments) with IS NULL (tests for NULL)

= NULL always evaluates to unknown/false, never true

questions.title: Diagnosing an accidental Cartesian product
questions.prompt: A query joining a 500-row Products table to a 100,000-row OrderDetail table unexpectedly returns 50 million rows instead of something in the few-hundred-thousand range. What almost certainly went wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: 50 million is exactly 500 times 100,000 -- the row-count signature of a Cartesian product, where every row of one table gets paired with every row of the other instead of only matching rows being paired. The most common real-world cause isn't a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- it's a missing or ineffective ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join: either the ON clause is left out entirely (old-style comma join with no join condition), or it exists but evaluates to true for nearly every row combination (for example ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which doesn't actually relate the two tables). To confirm it, check the join's ON clause first for a missing or non-relating condition, and as a general habit, sanity-check the row count after any join: if two tables of roughly 500 and 100,000 rows produce millions of result rows instead of a number in that rough range, that's an immediate signal to re-check the ON clause rather than assume the data is simply that large.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd notice is that 50 million is suspiciously close to 500 times 100,000 -- that's the fingerprint of a Cartesian product, not a coincidence. My first move is to go straight to the ON clause of the join and check two things: is it missing entirely, which happens with old comma-style joins that have no join condition at all, or does it exist but not actually relate the two tables -- something like ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which is true for almost every row and produces a Cartesian product in disguise even though there's technically an ON clause sitting there. Once I fix the condition to something that actually ties the tables together, like p.ProductID = sod.ProductID, I'd re-run the query and expect the row count to land in the same rough range as the bigger of the two tables, not multiply them together. I've made this a habit on every join I write now: sanity-check the row count before trusting the result.
questions.example:
-- BUG: no join condition at all -- a Cartesian product
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p, Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod;

-- BUG: ON clause exists but doesn't relate the tables
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.Name IS NOT NULL;

-- FIXED: a real join condition tying the tables together
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is just 'that big' instead of suspecting the join condition first
Not recognizing that an ON clause can exist and still produce a Cartesian product if it doesn't genuinely relate the tables
Never sanity-checking row counts after writing a join, so the problem isn't caught until it hits production
Confusing this with a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- the accidental version almost always comes from a broken or missing ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
keyPoints: Row count multiplying (500 x 100,000) instead of adding is the signature of a Cartesian product

questions.title: Inflated totals after a new relationship
questions.prompt: A Power BI report's total sales figure looks inflated after a new relationship was added between two tables, and that relationship's cardinality was automatically set to 'one to one.' What might be wrong, and how would incorrect cardinality cause this?
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI sets cardinality to one-to-one automatically when it notices a value never repeats on either side of the relationship at the time the relationship is created. If the underlying data later changes so that one side starts legitimately repeating values (for example, a second budget row gets added for the same project in a later refresh), that one-to-one relationship no longer reflects reality, and Power BI's query engine will treat each row match as unique when it isn't -- a many-side table with duplicated keys joined as if it were one-to-one can fan out matching rows and inflate a SUM measure, because the engine isn't aggregating correctly across what are actually multiple matching rows per key. The fix is to open Manage relationships, edit the relationship, and override the cardinality to 'many to one' (or 'one to many'), explicitly pointing the 'many' side at the table that actually repeats values, rather than trusting Power BI's automatic detection once the data's shape has changed.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move would be Manage relationships, to actually see what cardinality Power BI chose and why. One-to-one only gets picked automatically because, at the moment the relationship was created, Power BI genuinely didn't see any repeated values on either side -- but that's a snapshot of the data at one point in time, not a guarantee. If a later refresh adds a second row for the same key on one side -- say a second budget line for a project that used to have exactly one -- the relationship is now lying about the data's actual shape, and a SUM measure built on top of it can double-count or otherwise misbehave because the engine is still treating the join as strictly one-to-one. The fix is straightforward once I've diagnosed it: edit the relationship and explicitly set cardinality to many-to-one, with the 'many' side pointed at whichever table I know will eventually repeat values, rather than leaving it to Power BI's automatic guess.

Not realizing one-to-one is only ever a snapshot judgment based on the data present when the relationship was created
Looking everywhere except Manage relationships when a total looks wrong after a schema change
Not knowing which side of a mismatched relationship should be set to 'many'

If repeats appear later, a stale one-to-one relationship can cause incorrect aggregation
Check and, if needed, manually override cardinality in Manage relationships
Point the 'many' side at whichever table is known to eventually repeat values

questions.title: A slicer that silently doesn't filter
questions.prompt: A Power BI model has two relationships between the Sales table and the Date table -- one on OrderDate and one on ShipDate. A slicer built on the Date table filters visuals using OrderDate correctly, but a separate visual that's supposed to use ShipDate doesn't react to the slicer at all. What's almost certainly going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI only allows one active relationship between any two given tables at a time, so that every filter path through the model stays unambiguous. With two relationships between Sales and Date (OrderDate and ShipDate), only one can be active (shown as a solid line); the other is automatically made inactive (a dashed line in the model view) and does not propagate filters on its own at all -- a slicer built on Date simply has no effect on anything meant to rely on the inactive relationship. Editing the relationship to make ShipDate active wouldn't fix this -- it would just flip which relationship is inactive, since the one-active-at-a-time rule doesn't go away. The real fix is a measure that explicitly activates the inactive relationship for just that calculation: CALCULATE(<expression>, USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date])). Any visual that needs to filter by ShipDate has to use a measure built with USERELATIONSHIP; a plain SUM(Sales[Amount]) dropped into a visual keeps using whichever relationship is active, regardless of which date field happens to be on that visual's axis.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dashed line in the model view is the first thing I'd check, because that's Power BI's visual signal for an inactive relationship. Two relationships between the same pair of tables means only one gets to be active -- that's not a bug, it's by design, so there's always exactly one unambiguous filter path between any two tables. Flipping which one is active in Manage Relationships doesn't actually solve this; it just swaps which one is now inactive. What I'd do instead is write a measure specifically for the ShipDate-based visual using CALCULATE with USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date]) wrapped around it, which activates that relationship for just this one calculation. A plain SUM measure on that same visual would still silently follow the active OrderDate relationship no matter what's on the axis, which is exactly the confusing symptom described here.
questions.example:
-- Ship Date Sales = CALCULATE(
--     SUM(Sales[Amount]),
--     USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date])
-- )
-- Activates the normally-inactive ShipDate relationship for just this measure.
commonMistakes: Trying to make the ShipDate relationship active in Manage Relationships, not realizing that just makes OrderDate inactive instead -- only one can be active at a time
Not noticing the dashed line in the model diagram, which is Power BI's visual signal for an inactive relationship
Assuming a visual will automatically use the 'other' relationship just because that date field is on the visual's axis
Forgetting USERELATIONSHIP only works inside CALCULATE, and only activates the relationship for that one measure's evaluation
keyPoints: Power BI allows only one active relationship between any two tables at a time
The second relationship becomes inactive automatically, shown as a dashed line
An inactive relationship does not propagate filters until explicitly activated
USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE activates an inactive relationship for one measure's calculation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the inactive-relationship cause
Correctly explains why only one relationship can be active
Proposes the correct fix (USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE)

questions.title: SUM inflated after joining a one-to-many table
questions.prompt: A query joins SalesOrderHeader to SalesOrderDetail and correctly totals each order with SUM(LineTotal). After adding a third join to a Promotion table -- where some orders have more than one matching promotion row -- the total for those specific orders suddenly doubles or triples, even though nothing about the actual sales changed. The join conditions are all correct and genuinely relate the tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a Cartesian product -- every join condition is correct and genuinely relates the tables -- it's join fan-out, which happens whenever a correct join still has a one-to-many relationship on one side. Each SalesOrderDetail row that matches more than one Promotion row gets physically duplicated once per matching promotion before SUM ever runs, so SUM(LineTotal) is now adding the same line total two or three times for any order whose promotion happens to match more than once, while orders with exactly one (or zero) matching promotions are unaffected. The fix is to never combine two separate one-to-many expansions in a single flat join and then aggregate at the end -- instead, pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the grain actually needed, in its own subquery or CTE, before joining. Here, that means computing the order total from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail alone first, and only joining Promotion afterward (or in a separate query) if promotion details are genuinely needed, rather than letting its fan-out multiply rows that feed directly into the order-total SUM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that this isn't the Cartesian-product bug people usually learn about -- every join condition here is correct and really does relate the tables. This is fan-out: joining in a table that can legitimately match more than one row per order duplicates the order-detail rows underneath it, once per matching promotion, before the SUM even runs. So an order with two matching promotions gets its LineTotal counted twice, not because the math is wrong, but because the row genuinely got duplicated first. My fix is to separate the two aggregations: compute each order's total from just SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail in a CTE first, completely isolated from the Promotion join, and only bring Promotion into a separate query (or join it after the order total is already locked in) if I actually need promotion-level detail. The rule I'd apply going forward is never to let two independent one-to-many joins sit in the same flat query feeding one aggregate -- pre-aggregate each one to the grain I need first.
questions.example:
-- WRONG: Promotion's fan-out inflates the order total
SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
JOIN Sales.SpecialOfferProduct promo ON promo.ProductID = sod.ProductID
GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID;

-- FIXED: order total computed in isolation, before any promotion join
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
    JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
    GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID
)
SELECT * FROM OrderTotals;
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct, relating join condition rules out row duplication entirely
Not comparing row counts (or a known-good total) before and after adding the third join
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT ...) as a quick fix, which only coincidentally works and breaks again as soon as two genuinely different line totals happen to match
Combining two separate one-to-many expansions in one flat query feeding a single aggregate, instead of pre-aggregating each one to the grain actually needed
keyPoints: A correct join condition can still fan out rows when the relationship is genuinely one-to-many
Fan-out duplicates rows before aggregation runs, inflating any SUM downstream
This is distinct from a Cartesian product, which comes from a missing or non-relating join condition
Fix: pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the needed grain in its own subquery/CTE before joining further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fan-out (not a Cartesian product)
Explains why the duplication inflates the SUM
Proposes a correct fix (pre-aggregating before joining further)

questions.title: Numbers doubled after joining two tables
questions.prompt: After joining an Orders table to a Returns table in Tableau, total Sales for every order that has at least one matching return has doubled, even though the join field (OrderID) is correct and genuinely relates the two tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a granularity mismatch, not a wrong join key. Orders has one row per order, but Returns can have more than one row per OrderID (one row per individual returned item). A standard join matches on OrderID, and any order with two return rows gets its order row duplicated once per matching return row before any aggregation runs -- so SUM(Sales) on that duplicated data counts the same order's Sales value twice (or more). The join condition itself is correct; the problem is combining two tables at different grains (one row per order vs. one row per returned item) with a row-level join and then aggregating the finer-grained measure. The fix is to either use Tableau's Relationships (instead of a row-level Join) for this combination, since relationships preserve each table's native grain and only aggregate at query time rather than physically duplicating rows up front, or to pre-aggregate the Returns table to one row per OrderID (for example, a count of returns per order) before joining it to Orders at the order grain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain that OrderID being the right join field doesn't rule out this bug -- the problem is grain, not the join key. Orders has one row per order; Returns can have several rows per order if more than one item got returned. A row-level join matches on OrderID and physically duplicates the Orders row once per matching Returns row before Sales ever gets summed, so an order with two returns has its Sales value counted twice. My first fix would be to switch from a physical Join to a Tableau Relationship for this pair of tables, since relationships keep each table at its own native grain and aggregate correctly at query time instead of flattening and duplicating rows up front. If a Join is specifically required for some other reason, the alternative is to pre-aggregate Returns down to one row per OrderID first -- say, a return count -- before joining it to Orders, so the join itself never multiplies anything.
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct join key (OrderID) rules out row duplication
Not checking whether the second table actually has more than one row per join key
Reaching for a Join when a Relationship would preserve each table's native grain instead
Not noticing the doubled totals only affect orders that actually have a matching return row
keyPoints: A correct join key doesn't rule out row duplication if the two tables are at different grains
A physical join duplicates rows before aggregation when the joined table has multiple matches per key
Tableau Relationships preserve each table's native grain instead of flattening/duplicating
Alternative fix: pre-aggregate the finer-grained table to the coarser grain before joining

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the grain mismatch as the cause, not the join key
Explains how row duplication inflates the aggregate
Proposes a correct fix (Relationships or pre-aggregation)
