questions.title: A dashboard that takes 30 seconds to load
questions.prompt: A Tableau dashboard with six worksheets and a dozen filters takes nearly 30 seconds to load, and users are complaining. What are the most likely causes, and in what order would you investigate them?
questions.modelAnswer: Check the connection type first, since it's usually the single biggest factor: a live connection re-queries the underlying database every time a filter changes or the dashboard loads, so performance is capped by the source database's own speed, while an extract is a compressed, Tableau-optimized local copy of the data that's almost always faster for this kind of interactive dashboard. If it's already an extract, the next check is how many worksheets and filters are actually on the dashboard at once -- each visible worksheet runs its own query, and context filters in particular force an extra internal temp-table step that's expensive if used on something that changes often. Also worth checking: are calculated fields doing row-level work that could be pre-computed once at the data-source level instead of recalculated by every worksheet, and is the dashboard applying filters to all six worksheets simultaneously when some of them don't actually need all twelve filters applied. The investigation order is: connection type (live vs. extract) first, since it's the largest lever, then worksheet/filter count and context filter usage, then calculated-field efficiency.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question is always live connection or extract, because that one setting usually explains more of the slowness than anything else -- a live connection means every filter click re-runs a query against the source database, while an extract is a local, compressed copy built for exactly this kind of interactive use. If it's already an extract and still slow, I'd look at how many worksheets are actually rendering at once -- six is a lot for one dashboard -- and whether any of the twelve filters are set as context filters, since those force Tableau to build an internal temp table every time they change, which is expensive if that filter gets touched often. I'd also check whether some of those filters are even relevant to all six worksheets, since applying every filter to every sheet by default can force worksheets to recompute that didn't actually need to. I'd work through it in that order -- connection type, then filter/worksheet load, then calculation efficiency -- because connection type alone is usually the biggest single fix.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to rewriting calculated fields before checking the much bigger live-vs-extract factor
Not knowing context filters are more expensive than regular filters because of the internal temp-table step
Applying every dashboard filter to every worksheet by default, even ones that don't need it
Assuming more worksheets always means proportionally more load time, without checking which ones are actually expensive
keyPoints: Live connection vs. extract is usually the single biggest performance factor
Each worksheet on a dashboard runs its own query; six active worksheets is a meaningful load
Context filters are more expensive than regular filters due to an internal temp-table step
Investigate connection type first, then filter/worksheet load, then calculation efficiency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies live vs. extract as the primary lever
Correctly identifies filter/worksheet load and context filter cost
Gives a sensible investigation order

questions.title: VLOOKUP returns a value, but the wrong one
questions.prompt: A VLOOKUP formula runs without any error and returns a price for every product, but several of the prices are wrong for products whose IDs aren't sorted in the lookup table. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is the missing (or mistakenly TRUE) fourth argument on VLOOKUP, which controls match type. VLOOKUP's match-type argument defaults to TRUE (approximate match) if it's left out entirely, and an approximate match requires the lookup column to be sorted ascending -- if it isn't, TRUE match returns whatever the approximate-match algorithm lands on, which can be a completely unrelated row, and it does this without raising any error, since from VLOOKUP's point of view it did find 'a' match, just not an exact one. The fix is to add FALSE as the fourth argument, forcing an exact match only -- if an exact ID isn't found, it correctly returns #N/A instead of a wrong-but-plausible value. This is also exactly the kind of bug XLOOKUP avoids by defaulting to exact match in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move would be to check the formula's fourth argument. If it's missing, VLOOKUP defaults to approximate match, which only behaves correctly if the lookup column is sorted ascending -- and the question already says it isn't. With an unsorted column and approximate match, VLOOKUP doesn't throw an error, it just confidently returns whatever row its approximate-match algorithm happens to land on, which is often a completely different product's price. The fix is adding FALSE explicitly: =VLOOKUP(A2, LookupTable, 2, FALSE). That change alone would make a genuinely missing ID show #N/A instead of silently returning a wrong number, which is actually the more useful outcome -- a visible error you can investigate, instead of a wrong number you might not catch.
questions.example:
-- WRONG (or missing 4th argument): approximate match on unsorted data
=VLOOKUP(A2, LookupTable, 2, TRUE)

-- FIXED: forces exact match
=VLOOKUP(A2, LookupTable, 2, FALSE)
commonMistakes: Leaving out the fourth argument entirely, silently defaulting to approximate match
Assuming VLOOKUP always throws a visible error when something is wrong
Not checking whether the lookup column is actually sorted before trusting an approximate match
Not recognizing XLOOKUP's exact-match default would have avoided this entire class of bug
keyPoints: VLOOKUP defaults to approximate match (TRUE) if the fourth argument is omitted
Approximate match requires the lookup column to be sorted ascending to behave sensibly
An unsorted column with approximate match returns a wrong value with no error at all
Adding FALSE forces exact match, surfacing a genuine miss as #N/A instead of a wrong number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the missing/incorrect match-type argument
Explains why approximate match misbehaves on unsorted data
Gives the correct fix

questions.title: New rows aren't showing up in a PivotTable
questions.prompt: Ten new rows were added to the bottom of a dataset, and after clicking Refresh, a PivotTable built from that data still doesn't include them. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix it going forward so this doesn't keep happening?
questions.modelAnswer: Refresh updates the PivotTable's values using its existing source range, but it doesn't expand that range on its own -- if the PivotTable was built from a fixed range reference (like Sheet1!A1:D200) instead of a structured Excel Table, adding rows below row 200 adds them outside the range the PivotTable is even looking at, so Refresh correctly reports nothing new to update because, as far as the PivotTable knows, nothing in its source range changed. The permanent fix is to convert the source data to an Excel Table (Ctrl+T) and rebuild (or edit) the PivotTable to point at that Table by name instead of a fixed range -- a Table automatically grows to include new rows added directly beneath it, so the PivotTable's source range grows along with it on every future refresh, with no manual range editing ever needed again.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd check what the PivotTable's actual source is first -- PivotTable Analyze -> Change Data Source will show it. If it's a hard-coded range like A1:D200, that's almost certainly the issue: Refresh only recalculates against whatever range is already defined, it doesn't notice rows added past the end of that range at all. The one-time fix for today is editing that range to include the new rows. The fix that actually prevents this from recurring is converting the source to a real Excel Table with Ctrl+T and pointing the PivotTable at the Table's name instead of a fixed range -- a Table expands automatically as rows are added directly below it, so every future refresh just works without me ever touching the range reference again.
commonMistakes: Assuming Refresh will automatically notice rows added outside the PivotTable's current source range
Manually re-editing the range after every batch of new rows instead of fixing the root cause
Not checking Change Data Source to see what range the PivotTable is actually pointed at
Converting to a Table but forgetting to update the existing PivotTable to point at the Table's name
keyPoints: Refresh only recalculates against the PivotTable's existing source range -- it doesn't expand that range
A fixed range reference as the source is the most common cause of this symptom
Converting the source to an Excel Table makes the range expand automatically as rows are added
Change Data Source shows what range/Table a PivotTable is actually built from

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the fixed-range source as the cause
Gives a correct immediate fix
Gives a correct permanent fix (convert to Table)

questions.title: A pandas merge is producing unexpected NaNs
questions.prompt: You merge two DataFrames on a CustomerID column, and most rows come back fine, but a chunk of rows that should have matched instead show NaN for every column from the second DataFrame. What are the most likely causes, and how would you check which one it is?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause is a data type or formatting mismatch in the join key between the two DataFrames -- for example, CustomerID stored as an integer (1024) in one DataFrame but as a string with leading characters or whitespace ('1024 ', 'CUST-1024') in the other. Because merge compares values for an exact match, '1024' (string) and 1024 (integer) are never considered equal even though they represent the same customer, so pandas correctly reports no match and fills the row with NaN rather than erroring. To check, compare df1["CustomerID"].dtype against df2["CustomerID"].dtype directly, and inspect a handful of the specific values that failed to match (not just a random sample) for stray whitespace, inconsistent casing, or a prefix that one side has and the other doesn't. The fix depends on what's found: casting both columns to the same type with .astype(str) (or int), and/or stripping whitespace with .str.strip(), before merging.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always to check dtypes on both sides -- df1["CustomerID"].dtype and df2["CustomerID"].dtype -- because a mismatch there, like one side being int64 and the other being object (string), means merge will never consider '1024' and 1024 equal, even though they're obviously the same customer to a person reading the sheet. If the types already match, my next check is whitespace or formatting on the specific values that failed, not a random sample -- I'd filter down to exactly the rows that came back NaN and print their CustomerID values raw, since a trailing space or a stray prefix like 'CUST-' is invisible when you're just eyeballing a printed DataFrame. Once I know which one it is, the fix is usually one line: casting both columns to the same type with .astype(str), or stripping whitespace with .str.strip(), before the merge runs.
questions.example:
print(df1["CustomerID"].dtype, df2["CustomerID"].dtype)

# Normalize both sides before merging
df1["CustomerID"] = df1["CustomerID"].astype(str).str.strip()
df2["CustomerID"] = df2["CustomerID"].astype(str).str.strip()
merged = df1.merge(df2, on="CustomerID", how="left")

Checking a random sample of rows instead of specifically the rows that failed to match
Casting only one side's column type and not the other
Not checking for invisible whitespace, which looks identical to the eye but fails an exact-match comparison
keyPoints: A type mismatch in the join key (e.g. int vs. string) causes merge to silently fail to match, producing NaN
Check df.dtype on both join columns as the first diagnostic step
Inspect the specific failed rows for whitespace or formatting differences, not a random sample
Fix by normalizing both columns to the same type/format before merging

Describes a correct diagnostic approach (dtype check, inspecting failed rows)
Gives a correct fix

questions.title: Power BI Desktop vs. the Power BI Service
questions.prompt: What's the architectural difference between Power BI Desktop and the Power BI Service, and why does a report usually need both instead of just one or the other?
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI Desktop is a free, locally-installed Windows application where all of the authoring happens -- connecting to data sources, building the data model and DAX measures in Power Query and the model view, and designing the actual report visuals. It produces a single .pbix file that lives on the author's own machine until it's deliberately published. The Power BI Service (app.powerbi.com) is the cloud-hosted side -- a published report lives inside a workspace there, where it can be shared with other people, scheduled for automatic data refresh, organized into an App for wider distribution, and secured with row-level security role assignments. The split exists because authoring (building a model, writing measures, designing visuals) and consumption/distribution (viewing, sharing, scheduling, securing) are genuinely different jobs with different audiences: one author builds in Desktop, then publishes once to the Service so many viewers can consume it without ever touching Desktop or the underlying model. Some things can only happen in the Service (scheduled refresh against on-premises data via a gateway, app distribution, RLS role assignment) and some only in Desktop (building or materially changing the data model) -- which is exactly why most real projects move back and forth between the two rather than picking only one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe Desktop as the workshop and the Service as the storefront. Desktop is where I actually build things -- the model, the measures, the report layout -- all saved into one .pbix file that nobody else can see until I choose to publish it. The Service is where that finished work actually reaches people: it lives in a workspace, it can be shared, it can be scheduled to refresh on its own overnight, and it's the only place I can assign a specific person to a row-level-security role. I couldn't do RLS assignment or scheduled refresh from inside Desktop even if I wanted to -- those are Service-only capabilities -- and I can't materially change the data model from inside the Service, so a real change still has to start back in Desktop and get republished. That back-and-forth isn't a workaround, it's just how the two pieces are meant to work together.

Trying to assign RLS role membership inside Desktop, which isn't possible there
Forgetting a report has to be deliberately published from Desktop before it exists in the Service at all
Not realizing scheduled, unattended data refresh is a Service feature, not something Desktop does on its own
keyPoints: Power BI Desktop: local authoring tool, produces a .pbix file, where the model and visuals are built
Power BI Service: cloud hosting/distribution layer -- sharing, scheduled refresh, apps, RLS assignment
Authoring and distribution are different jobs with different audiences
Some features exist only in Desktop (model building) and some only in the Service (RLS assignment, scheduled refresh, apps)

questions.title: Why Dev, QA, and Production stay separate
questions.prompt: Why does a BI team typically maintain separate Dev, QA, and Production SQL Server environments, and promote a change through them in that fixed order, instead of just building and testing directly against the Production database that live reports and real users already depend on?
questions.modelAnswer: Dev is where new work is actually built, and it's expected to be unstable -- half-finished packages, broken queries, and throwaway test data are all normal there, and critically, none of that instability is visible to anyone who depends on real numbers. QA is a separate, more stable environment with data that resembles Production, used specifically to verify a change behaves correctly before any real user is ever exposed to it -- this is where testing is supposed to happen, not in Dev and not in Production. Production is the environment real business users and live reports actually run against, and it's deliberately the last environment any change reaches, only after being built in Dev and then validated in QA. Testing directly against Production is risky for two concrete reasons: an in-progress or buggy change can lock, corrupt, or simply show wrong numbers in data that live reports depend on right now, and there's no safe way to test something genuinely risky -- a schema change, a large bulk load -- without potentially causing a real outage if it goes wrong. Promoting a change through Dev, then QA, then Production in that fixed order guarantees every change gets at least one chance to fail somewhere that doesn't matter yet before it ever reaches somewhere that does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what's allowed to break where. Dev is allowed to break -- that's the whole point of it, it's where I'm actively building and nobody real is looking at it. QA is where I prove a change actually works against data that looks like the real thing, before any real user sees it. Production is the one environment where breaking something has an actual business cost, so it's deliberately the last stop, not the first. If I skipped straight to testing in Production, the two real risks are: a change that's still buggy could corrupt or lock data that a live report is reading from right now, and there's no safe way to rehearse something genuinely risky, like a schema change, without actually risking the outage I was trying to avoid. The fixed Dev-then-QA-then-Production order is really just making sure every change gets tested somewhere low-stakes before it reaches somewhere high-stakes.
commonMistakes: Making a direct change in Production 'just this once' to save time
Treating QA as optional for a change that 'seems small' instead of validating it there first
Letting QA's data drift so far from Production's that it stops catching real issues
Conflating Dev and QA as the same environment instead of recognizing their different purposes (building vs. validating)
keyPoints: Dev is for building and is expected to be unstable, isolated from real users
QA validates a change against production-like data before any real user is exposed to it
Production is the last environment reached, only after Dev and QA
Direct Production changes risk live data and can't safely rehearse risky operations

questions.title: Why the semantic model is its own layer
questions.prompt: In Power BI, what is a semantic model (also called a dataset), and why is it treated as a layer separate from any one report built on top of it? What becomes possible once you realize several different reports can all point at the very same semantic model?
questions.modelAnswer: A semantic model is the published data model itself -- tables, relationships, calculated columns, measures, and RLS roles -- without any particular report's visuals attached to it; it's the single source of truth layer sitting between raw data and however many reports choose to visualize it. Publishing a single .pbix that has both a model and report visuals does create a semantic model and a report together by default, but once published, the semantic model exists in the workspace as its own independent object. Any report author with the right permission can then build a brand-new report connected to that existing semantic model (through Create report, or a Live Connection) without rebuilding the tables, relationships, or measures from scratch. This matters because it means business logic -- how a measure is calculated, which relationships are correct, who can see which rows under RLS -- is defined exactly once, and every report built against that semantic model automatically inherits the same correct logic; if a measure's definition ever needs fixing, fixing it once in the semantic model updates every report built on top of it, instead of requiring the same fix to be found and repeated across several separately-built reports.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the semantic model as the thing that actually has the business logic in it -- the relationships, the measures, the RLS roles -- completely separate from however a given report chooses to visualize that logic. Publishing one .pbix does hand you both a semantic model and a report at the same time, but they're two separate objects the moment they land in the workspace, and that's exactly what lets a finance team build one report and an executive-summary team build a completely different-looking report, both connected live to that same underlying semantic model, without either of them re-deriving what 'Total Revenue' actually means. The real payoff is maintenance: if I find a bug in a measure, I fix it once, in the semantic model, and every report built on top of it -- including ones I didn't build myself -- picks up the fix automatically, instead of me having to track down and patch the same formula in five separate files.
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the same measures and relationships from scratch in every new report instead of connecting to the existing semantic model
Thinking a published semantic model and a published report are the same object
Not realizing RLS lives on the semantic model, so it applies consistently to every report connected to it
Forgetting a Live Connection report depends on that semantic model staying published and accessible
keyPoints: A semantic model is the data model (tables, relationships, measures, RLS) without any one report's visuals
Publishing a .pbix creates a semantic model and a report, but they become separate objects in the workspace
Multiple reports can connect to one shared semantic model via Live Connection
Fixing logic once in the semantic model updates every report built on top of it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a semantic model and what it contains
Correctly explains that it's a separate object from any one report
Explains the maintenance/consistency benefit of multiple reports sharing one model

questions.title: Relationships vs. Joins vs. Blending in Tableau
questions.prompt: Tableau gives you three different ways to combine data from two tables or data sources: Relationships, Joins, and Data Blending. At a high level, when would you reach for each one?
questions.modelAnswer: Relationships are Tableau's modern default for combining tables within the same data source -- they keep each table at its own native level of detail and only combine rows at query time, based on which fields are actually in the current view, which avoids the row-duplication/fan-out risk a physical join can create when tables are at different grains. A Join physically combines two tables into one flat table at the data-source level before any analysis happens, which is appropriate when you genuinely want one single flattened table and you've confirmed the two tables are at a compatible grain. Data Blending is reserved for combining two genuinely separate data sources (for example, an Excel file and a live SQL Server connection) that can't be connected as a Relationship or Join at all because they're not part of the same connection -- it works at the aggregate level (post-aggregation), which makes it noticeably more limited than a Relationship or Join and prone to its own quirks if the linking field doesn't aggregate the same way on both sides. The practical order of preference for two tables in the same source is: Relationship first, Join only when a genuinely flat single table is actually wanted, and Blending only when the two sources truly can't be connected any other way.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default to a Relationship for two tables that live in the same connection, since it's built specifically to avoid the grain-mismatch row-duplication problem that a physical Join can create -- it keeps each table at its own level of detail and only combines them at query time based on what's actually in the view. I'd reach for an actual Join only when I specifically want one flattened table and I've already confirmed the two tables are at a compatible grain, since a Join does combine everything up front, duplication risk included. Blending is the one I use least, and only when there's genuinely no other option -- two separate data sources, like an Excel file and a live database connection, that can't be connected as a Relationship or Join because they're not even part of the same connection. Blending works after aggregation has already happened on each side, which makes it noticeably more limited, so it's a last resort, not a first choice.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a physical Join when a Relationship would avoid the row-duplication risk entirely
Not realizing Blending only works across genuinely separate data sources, not two tables already in one connection
Forgetting Blending operates after aggregation, which limits what it can do compared to a Relationship or Join
Assuming the three options are interchangeable rather than fitting different specific situations
keyPoints: Relationships: default for same-source tables, preserve native grain, combine at query time
Joins: physically flatten two tables up front, fine when grain is compatible and one flat table is wanted
Blending: last resort for genuinely separate data sources, works post-aggregation
Preference order: Relationship, then Join, then Blending only when nothing else connects the sources

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the three approaches
Correctly explains when each is the right choice
Mentions Blending's post-aggregation limitation

questions.title: Choosing an extract vs. a live connection for a new dashboard
questions.prompt: You're designing a new Tableau dashboard. One stakeholder wants it refreshed nightly and fast to click through; another says they occasionally need to see numbers that are accurate to the last few minutes. How would you decide between a live connection and an extract, and is it necessarily an all-or-nothing choice?
questions.modelAnswer: For the first stakeholder's need -- a fast, interactive dashboard refreshed nightly -- an extract is the right architectural choice: it's a compressed, Tableau-optimized local copy of the data that loads and filters quickly regardless of how large or slow the source database is, and 'nightly' freshness is exactly what a scheduled extract refresh is built for. For the second stakeholder's need -- numbers accurate to the last few minutes -- a live connection is required, since an extract is only ever as fresh as its last refresh and cannot show true real-time data. It isn't necessarily all-or-nothing at the workbook level: Tableau supports having some data sources in a workbook set to live and others set as extracts, so a design that genuinely needs both could split the dashboard's heavier historical data into an extract for speed while keeping a smaller, specifically real-time data source (or a separate real-time-only view) on a live connection, rather than forcing the entire workbook into one mode that satisfies only one stakeholder.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd map each requirement to the tool built for it rather than trying to force one setting to satisfy both. The stakeholder who wants speed and is fine with nightly data is describing exactly what an extract is for -- a fast, local, compressed copy that doesn't care how slow the source database is, refreshed on a schedule. The stakeholder who needs minute-level accuracy is describing what a live connection is for, since an extract is only ever as fresh as its last scheduled refresh. I wouldn't assume I have to pick one setting for the whole workbook, though -- Tableau lets different data sources within the same workbook be live or extracted independently, so if there's a genuine need for both, I'd keep the bulk of the historical data as a fast extract and put only the specific real-time-sensitive piece on a live connection, rather than slowing down the entire dashboard to satisfy one occasional need.
commonMistakes: Assuming the whole workbook has to be either fully live or fully extracted
Choosing extract for speed without checking whether any part of the requirement genuinely needs real-time data
Choosing live connection everywhere 'to be safe' and accepting the performance cost unnecessarily
Not recognizing that scheduled nightly extract refresh is specifically built for the first stakeholder's stated need
keyPoints: Extract: fast, compressed, scheduled refresh -- fits a 'fast and refreshed nightly' requirement
Live connection: always current, but performance depends on the source -- fits a true real-time requirement
The choice isn't necessarily all-or-nothing at the workbook level
Different data sources within one workbook can independently be live or extracted

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps each stakeholder's need to the right connection type
Correctly identifies this isn't necessarily an all-or-nothing choice
Proposes a sensible mixed design

questions.title: Why build a view for BI tools to query, instead of pointing them at raw tables
questions.prompt: A BI team is about to connect Power BI and Tableau directly to raw transactional tables in the production database. Why would you instead recommend building a layer of views for those tools to query against, even though the views initially just mirror the raw tables with no extra logic?
questions.modelAnswer: A view sitting between raw tables and reporting tools creates a stable interface -- the reporting tools depend on the view's column names and shape, not on the underlying table's actual structure, so when the underlying schema needs to change later (a column renamed, a table split, logic added to compute a previously-raw value), the view can be updated to absorb that change while the view's own interface -- and every report built against it -- keeps working untouched. Without that layer, a schema change to a raw table breaks every report, dashboard, and connection pointed directly at it, often without warning until someone notices a broken refresh. Starting the view as a simple mirror with no extra logic yet doesn't waste the effort -- it's specifically about having that decoupling point already in place before it's needed, so the first time logic does need to be added (a calculated column, a renamed field, a filter excluding test data) it has an obvious, low-risk place to go without touching any report directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as decoupling, the same idea as an API sitting between a frontend and a database. If Power BI and Tableau both connect straight to the raw tables, every single report is now directly coupled to that table's exact current shape, and a schema change anywhere upstream breaks all of them at once, usually discovered only when someone notices a report stopped refreshing. If instead both tools connect to a thin view that currently just mirrors the table one-to-one, a future schema change gets absorbed inside the view -- update the view's definition once, and every report pointed at it keeps working without any of them being touched. Starting the view as a plain mirror isn't wasted effort; it's putting the seam in place now, while it's cheap, instead of trying to retrofit one later once a dozen reports are already connected directly to raw tables.
commonMistakes: Connecting reporting tools directly to raw tables because 'the view doesn't do anything yet anyway'
Assuming a decoupling layer is only worth building once logic is actually needed, not before
Not realizing a single upstream schema change can break every report connected directly to a raw table
Treating the view as a performance optimization instead of a stability/decoupling one
keyPoints: A view creates a stable interface between raw tables and reporting tools
Reports depend on the view's shape, not the underlying table's actual structure
A schema change can be absorbed inside the view without touching any downstream report
Building the decoupling layer early is cheaper than retrofitting it after many reports already connect directly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the decoupling/stable-interface concept
Explains the risk of connecting reporting tools directly to raw tables
Explains why building the view early (even as a simple mirror) has value

questions.title: Recognizing when a workbook has outgrown Excel
questions.prompt: A departmental Excel workbook with several linked sheets, a dozen PivotTables, and a handful of VLOOKUP chains has grown into something five people now edit and email around weekly. What are the warning signs that this has outgrown Excel, and what would you recommend moving it to?
questions.modelAnswer: The warning signs are less about file size and more about structural strain: multiple people editing the same file and emailing versions around means there's no single source of truth -- two people can easily be looking at different versions at the same time, and there's no real way to see who changed what. A dozen PivotTables and chained VLOOKUPs pointed at several linked sheets also means a lot of manual, repeat-every-week rebuilding of the same transformation logic by hand, with real risk of a broken reference or a stale copy-pasted range going unnoticed. The recommendation is to move the data model into Power BI: Power Query replaces the manual VLOOKUP chains with a repeatable, auditable transformation pipeline that reruns identically on every refresh, the model's relationships replace sheet-linking, a published semantic model becomes the one single source of truth that many people view (rather than many people editing their own copy), and scheduled refresh replaces the weekly manual email-around entirely. Excel itself doesn't need to disappear -- it's still a fine tool for ad hoc, personal analysis -- but a shared, weekly, multi-editor report like this one is a textbook case for moving to a governed Power BI model instead.
questions.professionalAnswer: The signal that actually worries me isn't the file size, it's 'five people edit it and email it around.' At that point there's no single source of truth -- everyone might be looking at a slightly different version, and if a number looks wrong, there's no real way to tell who last touched what. A dozen PivotTables and a chain of VLOOKUPs across linked sheets is also just a lot of manual, hand-rebuilt logic that someone has to redo correctly every single week, which is exactly the kind of repeatable transformation Power Query is built to automate once and rerun identically every time. My recommendation would be to move the underlying data into a proper Power BI model -- Power Query replaces the VLOOKUP chains, the data model's relationships replace the sheet-linking, and a published semantic model becomes the one thing everyone actually looks at, with scheduled refresh replacing the weekly email. I wouldn't say Excel is bad here -- it's just the wrong tool once something this collaborative and recurring outgrows a single file that multiple people are editing by hand.
commonMistakes: Treating file size as the main signal instead of the lack of a single source of truth
Assuming the fix is just 'a bigger/better Excel file' instead of a genuinely different architecture
Not recognizing that email-and-edit-around is itself the core problem, independent of the workbook's complexity
Dismissing Excel entirely instead of recognizing it's still fine for personal, non-shared analysis
keyPoints: Multiple editors + emailing versions around means there's no single source of truth
Manual, repeat-every-week VLOOKUP/PivotTable rebuilding signals a need for a repeatable pipeline
Power Query replaces manual lookups; the data model replaces sheet-linking; a semantic model replaces the 'one file' everyone edits
Excel remains fine for personal/ad hoc analysis -- the issue is specifically shared, recurring, multi-editor use

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the real warning signs (single source of truth, manual rework)
Recommends Power BI with a correct explanation of what replaces what
Avoids overstating that Excel itself is the problem

questions.title: Choosing the right tool for a multi-source, multi-viewer report
questions.prompt: A stakeholder needs a report pulling from three source systems, viewed by around 50 people across two regions who should only see their own region's numbers, refreshed automatically every morning. Walk through how you'd decide between building this in Excel, Power BI, or Tableau, and how the pieces would fit together end to end.
questions.modelAnswer: Excel is ruled out quickly for the core deliverable: there's no clean, native way to automatically restrict different viewers of the same file to different rows of data, and distributing an Excel file to 50 people with a scheduled automatic refresh isn't something Excel is built to manage on its own -- it's better suited to a single analyst's own working file than a governed, shared report for 50 viewers. Between Power BI and Tableau, both can technically connect to multiple sources, model relationships, and schedule a refresh, so the decision usually comes down to the organization's existing licensing, the team's existing skill set, and which platform the viewers already use for other reports -- there often isn't a strictly technical reason to prefer one over the other for a scenario like this. Whichever is chosen, the end-to-end architecture is the same shape: Power Query (or Tableau's data source step) connects to and shapes all three source systems into a single consistent model, row-level security (Power BI RLS roles, or Tableau's row-level security via a filter tied to viewer identity) restricts each region to its own rows at the model layer rather than relying on separate files per region, and a scheduled refresh (via a gateway if any source is on-premises) keeps the model current every morning before the first viewer opens it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd rule out Excel pretty quickly for the actual deliverable, not because Excel is a bad tool, but because this specific requirement -- 50 viewers, two regions each restricted to their own numbers, refreshed automatically -- isn't something Excel is built to manage; there's no clean row-level security model and no real way to safely automate a scheduled refresh and distribution to that many people. Between Power BI and Tableau, honestly, either one can do this -- connect to three sources, build one model, apply row-level security, schedule a refresh. If I had to pick, I'd look at what the organization already has licensed and what the viewers already use day to day, since re-training 50 people on a brand-new tool is its own cost. Whatever I pick, the architecture is the same: shape all three sources into one consistent model first, apply row-level security at the model layer so there's one file with built-in restrictions instead of two separate region-specific files to maintain, and set up a scheduled refresh (through a gateway if anything's on-premises) so the data's current before the first person opens it in the morning.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to Excel because it's familiar, without checking whether it can actually meet the row-level-security and scheduled-refresh requirements
Building two separate region-specific files instead of one model with row-level security
Treating the Power BI vs. Tableau choice as a technical question when it's often a licensing/skill-set one
Forgetting a gateway is needed if any of the three sources is on-premises rather than cloud-hosted
keyPoints: Excel is poorly suited here: no native row-level security, not built for scheduled refresh to 50 viewers
Power BI and Tableau can both technically satisfy this; the choice is often licensing/skill-set driven
Row-level security at the model layer replaces maintaining separate per-region files
A gateway is needed for scheduled refresh if any source system is on-premises

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rules out Excel with a sound reason
Correctly frames Power BI vs. Tableau as not primarily a technical decision here
Describes a correct end-to-end architecture (model, RLS, scheduled refresh/gateway)

questions.title: Where Python fits relative to Power Query and DAX
questions.prompt: In a Power BI project, you have three places you could put a given transformation: Power Query, a DAX measure, or a Python script. How do you decide which one a specific piece of logic belongs in?
questions.modelAnswer: The decision generally follows the stage of the pipeline the logic belongs to. Power Query is for shaping and cleaning data before it loads into the model -- removing columns, fixing data types, merging/appending tables, splitting or combining text -- anything that should happen once, at refresh time, to the raw data itself. DAX is for logic that depends on how the report is currently being viewed -- a measure that needs to recalculate as a user clicks through filters, slicers, or drill-downs, which Power Query has no concept of since it runs before any report interaction exists. Python earns its place specifically when a transformation is awkward or impossible in either -- complex text parsing with regular expressions, a statistical calculation Power Query's UI doesn't expose a step for, or pulling in a specialized library (for fuzzy matching, for example) -- and Python scripts can run as a step inside Power Query itself or power a custom visual, rather than requiring an entirely separate pipeline. The practical rule: try Power Query first for anything that's genuinely a one-time data shape/clean, try DAX for anything that needs to react to how the report is being viewed, and reach for Python only when a specific gap in those two tools has actually been hit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about which stage of the pipeline the logic naturally belongs to. If it's a one-time cleanup or reshaping of the raw data -- fixing a data type, splitting a column, merging two tables -- that's Power Query, because it runs once per refresh, before the model or any report interaction exists. If it needs to recalculate as someone clicks around the report -- changes based on a slicer, a filter, a drill-down -- that has to be DAX, since Power Query has already finished running by the time a user is interacting with anything. Python is the one I reach for least, and only when I've actually hit something Power Query or DAX genuinely can't do cleanly -- a regex-heavy text cleanup, or a statistical function neither tool exposes. I wouldn't default to Python out of familiarity with it; I'd try the other two first and only drop into a Python step inside Power Query once I've confirmed there's a real gap.
commonMistakes: Writing report-interactive logic in Power Query, where it can't react to filters or slicers at all
Writing a one-time data-cleaning step in DAX instead of Power Query, where it belongs
Reaching for Python by default instead of confirming Power Query/DAX genuinely can't do it
Not knowing a Python script can run as a step inside Power Query itself rather than needing a separate pipeline
keyPoints: Power Query: one-time shaping/cleaning of raw data before the model exists
DAX: logic that must recalculate based on current report interaction (filters, slicers, drill-downs)
Python: fills specific gaps neither tool covers (regex, specialized statistics/libraries)
Python can run as a step inside Power Query rather than requiring a separate pipeline

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Power Query's and DAX's roles
Correctly frames Python as filling specific gaps, not a default choice
Gives a believable example of where each belongs

questions.title: When a Power BI analyst needs a dedicated pipeline tool
questions.prompt: A Power BI dataset that used to refresh in Power Query within a few minutes has grown to pull from five source systems and now takes over two hours, and sometimes fails partway through. At what point does this stop being a Power Query problem and become a case for a dedicated data-pipeline tool like Azure Data Factory, and what would actually change architecturally?
questions.modelAnswer: Power Query is designed to shape data for a single Power BI model, running entirely inside that model's own refresh -- it has no real concept of orchestrating multiple independent extracts, retrying just the one source system that failed without rerunning everything else, or being monitored and alerted on separately from the Power BI report itself. The warning signs described -- five source systems, a refresh over two hours, and partial failures -- are signs the job has grown from 'shape this data for my report' into 'orchestrate an actual data pipeline,' which is a different problem than Power Query was built to solve. Azure Data Factory is purpose-built for that: it extracts from each of the five sources on its own schedule and its own retry logic, lands the combined, cleaned result into a staging table or warehouse, and only then does Power BI's Power Query step connect to that single, already-prepared destination -- a much lighter and more reliable refresh than pulling live from five separate systems every time. Architecturally, this moves the heavy lifting of extraction and orchestration upstream of Power BI entirely, leaving Power Query to do what it's actually good at: light, final-stage shaping of data that's already been consolidated.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say the warning sign isn't the hour count by itself, it's the combination -- five separate source systems and partial failures. Power Query refresh is really built to shape data for one model's own refresh cycle; it doesn't have a real way to retry just the one source that failed without redoing the other four, and it's not something I can monitor or alert on independently of the Power BI report itself. Once a refresh looks like 'orchestrate five different systems reliably,' that's a pipeline problem, not a shaping problem, and that's exactly the gap Azure Data Factory is built to fill -- it pulls from each source on its own schedule, with its own retry logic, and lands everything into one staging table or warehouse. At that point Power Query's job gets much lighter: it's just connecting to that one already-consolidated destination and doing final, light shaping, instead of trying to be the thing that pulls and orchestrates five sources every single refresh.

Assuming a slow refresh is always a Power Query optimization problem rather than an architecture problem
Not separating 'shaping data for one model' from 'reliably orchestrating multiple source systems'
Underestimating how much lighter Power Query becomes once it's pointed at one pre-consolidated destination instead of five live sources
keyPoints: Power Query is built to shape data for one model's refresh, not to orchestrate multiple independent sources with retry logic
Multiple sources + long runtime + partial failures signal an orchestration problem, not a shaping problem
Azure Data Factory extracts/orchestrates upstream and lands consolidated data into staging
After the move, Power Query only does light, final-stage shaping against one already-prepared destination

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the warning signs as an orchestration problem
Correctly explains what Data Factory does differently
Explains how Power Query's role changes afterward

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new BI team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. A junior new hire should resist the urge to over-explain or justify slow progress at length -- stand-up is meant to be short, and a longer conversation about a specific blocker belongs in a follow-up afterward, not consuming the whole meeting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the Lookup for the Customer dimension and started on the fact table load. Today I'm wiring up the error output so bad rows get redirected instead of failing the whole package. I'm blocked on getting read access to the QA staging database, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real ticket instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.
commonMistakes: Treating stand-up like a status report to a manager instead of the team syncing with itself
Being vague ('still working on it') instead of naming the specific ticket or task
Saving a blocker until later instead of surfacing it the moment it's identified
Turning stand-up into a long problem-solving discussion instead of flagging it briefly and following up afterward
keyPoints: Daily Scrum/stand-up is short, time-boxed, and team-to-team, not a report to a manager
Typical shape: what I did, what I'm doing next, what's blocking me
Name specific work, not vague progress statements
Surface blockers immediately; save detailed discussion for after stand-up

Gives a specific, well-structured example of what to say

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. I'd flag it the moment I realize it, specifically naming what I actually need to get unblocked, rather than just saying 'I'm stuck,' because a specific ask is what actually gets someone to act on it quickly.
commonMistakes: Quietly grinding on a ticket without flagging it, assuming asking for help makes you look unprepared
Mislabeling 'off track' (just taking longer) as 'blocked' when there's still personal progress possible
Waiting until the next stand-up to mention a blocker instead of flagging it the moment it's identified
Flagging a blocker vaguely instead of saying specifically what's needed to unblock it
keyPoints: Off Track: work is simply taking longer than planned, more time/closer look resolves it
Blocked: a hard stop entirely outside your control -- no amount of personal effort moves it forward
The test: is there anything I can still do myself right now? If no, you're blocked
Flag a blocker immediately and specifically, not quietly or vaguely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Off Track from Blocked

questions.title: Explaining why the team works in sprints, not all at once
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team can't just build the whole report and show it to them when it's completely done, instead of working in two-week sprints. How would you explain the difference between Agile and Waterfall to them, and why your team works the way it does?
questions.modelAnswer: Waterfall fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and fully understood up front, moving through fixed phases once in order -- but if a requirement turns out to be wrong, that's usually not discovered until most of the work is already built, which makes it expensive to fix at that point. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating two-week cycles, each one producing something real and working that the stakeholder can actually see and react to. The explanation should connect directly to the stakeholder's own interest rather than staying abstract: working in sprints means they get to say 'that's not quite what I meant' after two weeks of effort instead of after two months, which protects them, not just the team. It's also worth clarifying that a sprint still produces a genuinely working, shippable piece of the report each cycle -- not an unfinished fragment -- so showing it early isn't showing something broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip straight to what's in it for them. If we built the whole thing in one long pass and only showed it at the end, and it turned out we misunderstood something on day one, we wouldn't find that out until the entire report was already built -- which is expensive and slow to fix at that point. Working in two-week sprints means every two weeks you get to look at something real and tell us if we're headed the wrong direction, while that's still cheap to correct. I'd also be clear that what you're seeing every two weeks isn't a half-finished mess -- it's a genuinely working slice of the report, just not the whole thing yet. That's really the whole point of sprints: catching a misunderstanding in week two instead of week eight.
commonMistakes: Explaining Agile/Waterfall in the abstract without connecting it to why it benefits this stakeholder specifically
Implying sprints mean nothing gets fully finished, instead of explaining a sprint still produces a real, shippable increment
Being dismissive of the stakeholder's preference instead of explaining the real trade-off
Using unexplained jargon (backlog, increment, retrospective) instead of plain language
keyPoints: Waterfall fits stable, well-understood requirements but surfaces mistakes late and expensively
Agile's short cycles let the stakeholder react to real progress every 1-2 weeks, catching misunderstandings early
Connect the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest, not an abstract process lecture
Each sprint still produces a real, working increment, not an unfinished fragment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately explains the Agile vs. Waterfall trade-off

questions.title: Communicating during a live production incident
questions.prompt: Two days after a dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region all month. Walk me through how you'd investigate, and what you would communicate to the manager while you're still figuring out the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the two parts of this question clearly. On investigation: start with the simplest explanation before anything complex -- did the dashboard's scheduled refresh actually run last night at all -- then work backward from the visible symptom toward the source, checking whether the ETL load completed for that region, whether the issue is in the underlying data or just a report-level filter, rather than guessing at a cause. On communication: send an honest, specific acknowledgment quickly -- confirming the report was received, that it's being looked into, and giving a concrete time to expect an update -- rather than staying silent until a fix is confirmed. It's expected and professional to communicate while still investigating, not only once the cause is found; silence during that window reads as neglect even when real work is happening behind the scenes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into what I say and what I actually do, and do the communication part first. Within a few minutes I'd send something like: 'Thanks for flagging this -- I'm looking into it now and will have an update for you by end of day.' That costs me almost nothing and tells the manager they haven't been forgotten. Then I'd investigate from the simplest explanation outward: did last night's scheduled refresh actually complete, or did it fail silently? If the refresh ran fine, I'd check whether that region's rows actually loaded into the fact table for this month, or whether this is a filter or slicer issue purely inside the report itself. I'd keep narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source rather than guessing at something exotic first. Once I actually find the cause, I'd follow up with a clear explanation of what happened and what I changed -- not just a silent fix with no note at all.
commonMistakes: Staying silent until the fix is confirmed instead of acknowledging the report and giving a timeframe while still investigating
Jumping straight to a complex theory instead of checking the simplest thing first (did the scheduled refresh even run)
Investigating only inside the report itself without checking whether the issue actually originates further upstream in the data pipeline
Not giving the manager a concrete time to expect an update, leaving them to wonder if it's been forgotten
keyPoints: Communicate an acknowledgment and a timeframe immediately, don't wait for the fix to say anything
Investigate by narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source (refresh status, pipeline, source data)
Check the simplest explanation first (did the scheduled load actually run) before assuming something complex
Follow up with a clear explanation once the cause is found, not just a silent fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a logical investigation approach, working from symptom back to source
Correctly emphasizes communicating early, before the cause is known
Clarity and professionalism of the communication described

questions.title: Turning a vague business request into a user story
questions.prompt: A sales director emails you: 'Our regional managers keep asking me for last month's numbers by email. I need a dashboard that shows revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically, so they can check it themselves.' How would you turn that into a proper user story with acceptance criteria before you start building anything?
questions.modelAnswer: A user story is written from the user's point of view, in the shape 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' -- for this request: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' A story alone is too vague to know when it's actually done, which is what acceptance criteria are for -- specific, checkable conditions, such as 'the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning, with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's assigned territory.' Just as important is noticing what the original email left out: it never says what should happen when a region has zero sales for the month. A strong answer explicitly surfaces that gap -- either asking the sales director directly, or documenting a reasonable judgment call as its own acceptance criterion -- rather than silently guessing and discovering the wrong assumption after the dashboard is already built.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building from that email directly -- I'd turn it into a story first: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' Then I'd write acceptance criteria that are actually checkable, not just a vague sense of done -- something like 'reflects yesterday's closed sales by 7 AM with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's own territory.' The thing I'd specifically flag before writing a single line of DAX is that the email never says what should happen if a region had zero sales that month -- show it as zero, blank, or leave it off the list entirely? I'd either ask the sales director directly or write down my own reasonable assumption as an explicit acceptance criterion, because guessing silently on that detail is exactly the kind of thing that comes back wrong during UAT.
commonMistakes: Starting to build directly from the vague email instead of writing a structured user story first
Writing a user story with no acceptance criteria, leaving 'done' undefined
Silently guessing at an ambiguous detail (like the zero-sales case) instead of asking or explicitly documenting the judgment call
Writing acceptance criteria that aren't actually checkable ('looks good') instead of specific and testable
keyPoints: User story shape: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Acceptance criteria must be specific and checkable, not vague
Explicitly surface and resolve ambiguous details (like the zero-sales edge case) before building
A story isn't ready to build until its acceptance criteria are defined

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correctly-shaped user story
Writes specific, checkable acceptance criteria
Identifies and resolves an ambiguous detail from the original request

questions.title: Asking for help when you're stuck
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time early in a project when you didn't know how to do something and had to ask a teammate or a more senior developer for help. How did you approach that conversation, and what did you do with the answer afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing resourcefulness and whether a candidate can ask for help effectively, rather than either staying silently stuck or outsourcing the thinking entirely to someone else. A strong answer shows an attempt was made first -- checking documentation, trying an approach, forming a specific theory -- since teams value someone who tries before asking, but it should also show the candidate didn't stay stuck in silence for an unreasonably long time out of fear of looking unprepared. When actually asking, the question should be specific -- naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down -- rather than a vague 'it's not working,' since a specific question gets a faster and more useful answer. The Action should also cover what happened after getting the answer: not just copying the fix, but understanding why it worked, so the same category of problem doesn't require asking again. Result should state a concrete outcome using STAR -- being unblocked within some stated timeframe, and ideally applying the same concept independently on a later, similar problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story. Situation: early in my capstone, I couldn't get an OLE DB Destination's fast-load mode to actually speed anything up, and I'd already tried switching the data access mode and rereading the component's tooltips with no luck. Task: I needed to actually understand what I was missing, not just make the error go away. Action: I asked a more experienced developer a specific question -- 'I switched to fast load, but it's still inserting one row at a time based on the execution time, here's what I've already tried' -- rather than just saying it wasn't working. They pointed out I still had the destination's table lock option unchecked, which was serializing the insert behind other activity on the table. Result: once I checked that option, the load time dropped noticeably, and I started checking that same setting by default on every OLE DB Destination I've built since, without needing to ask again. I'd keep the story specific and make sure it lands on that last point -- what I actually learned to do differently afterward.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck in silence for too long before asking, out of fear of looking unprepared
Asking a vague question ('it's not working') instead of naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down
Copying the fix without understanding why it worked, so the same type of problem requires asking again later
Describing a general attitude toward asking for help instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Show an attempt was made before asking, but don't stay stuck in silence too long either
Ask a specific question naming what was tried and where it broke down
Understand why the answer worked rather than just copying it
Use STAR and state a concrete Result, including what changed afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows a reasonable attempt was made before asking for help
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result, including what was learned or applied afterward

questions.title: Two stakeholders define the same metric differently
questions.prompt: The VP of Sales and the VP of Finance both ask you for a 'Revenue' number on the same dashboard, but Sales counts a deal as revenue the day it's signed, while Finance counts it the day it's invoiced. How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer: The instinct to avoid is picking one definition quietly and hoping nobody notices, since that guarantees one VP eventually finds a number that doesn't match their own tracking and loses trust in the whole dashboard. The right first move is surfacing the conflict explicitly to both stakeholders (or whoever owns that decision) rather than resolving it unilaterally -- naming the actual difference in plain terms (signed date vs. invoiced date) and asking which one is the intended definition for this specific report, or whether the report genuinely needs to show both as two clearly labeled, separate measures. Once a decision is made, it needs to be documented, not just implemented silently -- a measure name like 'Revenue' is itself ambiguous, so renaming it to something explicit like 'Signed Revenue' and 'Invoiced Revenue' if both are kept, or adding a clear label/tooltip stating which definition is in use, prevents the same confusion from resurfacing later with a different viewer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't quietly pick one definition and hope it doesn't come up -- that's exactly the kind of thing that blows up later when Finance looks at the dashboard and the number doesn't match their own system. I'd go back to whoever actually owns this dashboard and lay out the conflict plainly: Sales means signed-date revenue, Finance means invoiced-date revenue, and those are genuinely two different numbers, not a rounding difference. Then I'd ask directly which one this report is supposed to show, or whether it needs both side by side as two separately labeled measures. Once that's decided, I wouldn't just build it and move on -- I'd make sure the label itself says which one it is, something like 'Signed Revenue' instead of just 'Revenue,' so six months from now nobody has to come ask me again which definition is on the dashboard.
commonMistakes: Quietly picking one definition without surfacing the conflict to either stakeholder
Resolving the conflict unilaterally instead of asking whoever owns the decision
Building both measures but leaving them both generically labeled 'Revenue,' recreating the same confusion
Treating this as a technical problem instead of a definitional/communication one
keyPoints: Surface a metric-definition conflict explicitly rather than resolving it quietly
Ask whoever owns the report which definition is intended, or whether both are needed
If both are kept, label them explicitly and distinctly, not generically
Document the decision so the same ambiguity doesn't resurface later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the conflict should be surfaced, not resolved silently
Describes a clear, professional way to raise it with stakeholders
Proposes a correct resolution (explicit labeling / documented decision)

questions.title: Explaining a data finding to a non-technical stakeholder
questions.prompt: You've found that a 15% drop in a region's reported sales last month was caused by a currency-conversion bug in the data pipeline, not an actual sales decline. How would you explain this to a regional VP who isn't technical, in a way that's accurate but doesn't lose them in the details?
questions.modelAnswer: The explanation should lead with the actual business-relevant conclusion first -- 'the 15% drop isn't real, it's a data error, and actual sales were roughly flat' -- rather than starting with a walkthrough of the currency-conversion logic, since a non-technical stakeholder's first and most urgent question is simply whether they should be worried, not how the bug works. After that headline, a short, plain-language explanation of the cause is appropriate (something converted at the wrong exchange rate before it reached the report), but the deeper technical detail -- which pipeline step, what exact code or query was wrong -- belongs in a follow-up for whoever will actually fix it, not in the stakeholder conversation. The explanation should also state what's being done about it and by when, since a non-technical stakeholder's second question is usually 'when will this be fixed,' and closing with a concrete timeframe avoids leaving that open.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lead with the headline, not the investigation: 'Good news -- that 15% drop wasn't real, it was a data error in how we were converting currency, and actual sales were close to flat.' That answers their most urgent question immediately instead of making them sit through a walkthrough of a pipeline bug before finding out whether they should actually be worried. Then I'd give one plain-language sentence on the cause -- something was converting at the wrong exchange rate before the number ever reached the report -- without getting into which specific step or query broke, since that detail matters to whoever's fixing it, not to them. I'd close with what's being done and by when, because the next question is always going to be 'when will this be fixed,' and I'd rather answer that up front than leave them to ask.
commonMistakes: Starting with the technical investigation instead of the business-relevant conclusion
Including unnecessary technical depth (specific code/query details) that doesn't help the stakeholder
Leaving out a concrete timeframe for when it'll be fixed
Being so simplified that the explanation becomes inaccurate rather than just appropriately high-level
keyPoints: Lead with the business-relevant conclusion, not the technical investigation
Keep the cause explanation in plain language, one or two sentences
Save deep technical detail for whoever will actually fix the issue, not the stakeholder conversation
Close with what's being done and a concrete timeframe

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with the conclusion the stakeholder actually cares about
Keeps the explanation accurate but appropriately non-technical
Includes next steps/timeframe

questions.title: Three urgent report requests on the same afternoon
questions.prompt: At 1 PM, three different teams each ask you for an urgent change to a report, all claiming they need it by end of day. You genuinely can't finish all three today. How do you decide what to do?
questions.modelAnswer: The first move is gathering enough information to actually prioritize rather than guessing or working in the order requests arrived -- for each request, roughly how long will it actually take, and what's the real consequence if it doesn't land today versus tomorrow (a board presentation happening today is materially different stakes than a routine weekly check someone would simply prefer sooner). That usually means a short, specific message to each requester -- not silence -- asking what the deadline is actually tied to, since 'I need it today' can mean genuinely different things across three people. Once that's known, the three requests can be ranked by actual business impact and effort, not by who asked first or loudest, and the people whose requests won't be finished today should be told proactively, with a specific time they can expect it, rather than letting them find out by simply not hearing back.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just start on whichever one landed in my inbox first -- I'd quickly message all three and ask what the deadline is actually tied to, because 'I need it today' from someone prepping for a board meeting this afternoon is a completely different situation from 'I need it today' meaning they'd just prefer not to wait until tomorrow. Once I know the real stakes and roughly how long each one will take, I can actually rank them by impact instead of by who asked loudest or first. Whoever's request isn't getting done today, I'd tell them that directly and as early as possible, with an actual time I'll have it instead -- not radio silence until they come looking for it, which is the version of this that actually damages trust.
commonMistakes: Working in the order requests arrived instead of gathering enough information to prioritize by actual impact
Assuming every 'urgent' claim carries the same weight without asking what it's actually tied to
Going silent on the requests that won't get done today instead of proactively communicating that
Trying to rush all three and doing a worse job on each instead of sequencing them deliberately
keyPoints: Gather real information (effort, actual stakes) before deciding priority, rather than guessing
Ask each requester what the deadline is actually tied to -- not all 'urgent' requests carry equal weight
Rank by actual business impact and effort, not by who asked first or loudest
Proactively tell anyone who won't be served today, with a specific new timeframe

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes gathering real information before prioritizing
Describes a sound prioritization approach based on impact
Addresses proactive communication with the deprioritized requesters

questions.title: Why move from Data Analyst toward BI Engineering
questions.prompt: You've been working as a Data Analyst. What's actually motivating you to grow into a BI Engineer role, and what have you been doing to build toward that?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer is specific about what actually changes between the two roles, not just a vague sense that BI Engineer 'sounds like a step up.' A Data Analyst typically works with data and models that already exist, answering business questions and building reports against them; a BI Engineer takes more ownership further upstream -- designing the data model itself, building and maintaining the pipelines and transformations that feed it, and being responsible for a report's reliability and performance, not just its content. A credible motivation names a specific experience that revealed that gap -- for example, repeatedly hitting the limits of what could be fixed inside a single report because the underlying model or data pipeline itself needed to change, and wanting to be the person who can make that change rather than only ever filing a request for someone else to make it. The second half of the answer should show concrete action already taken, not just intention -- specific skills being built (SQL beyond basic querying, data modeling, understanding how data gets from source systems into the model in the first place) rather than a general statement of enthusiasm.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific rather than giving the generic 'I want to grow' answer. What actually pushed me toward this was hitting a point, a few times, where a report had a real problem -- slow, or a number that was technically right but the model structure made it clunky to get at -- and the fix wasn't something I could make inside the report itself; it needed a change to the underlying data model or the way data was being loaded in the first place. I kept having to file that as a request for someone else and wait, and I realized I wanted to be the person who could actually make that fix. So I've been deliberately building the skills that sit upstream of where I was working before -- going deeper into SQL past basic querying, actually learning data modeling, understanding what it takes to build and maintain the pipeline that gets data into the model in the first place -- rather than just saying I want the title.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer about wanting to 'grow' without naming the actual difference between the two roles
Describing BI Engineering as just 'more advanced reporting' instead of upstream ownership (modeling, pipelines, reliability)
Stating interest without describing any concrete action already taken toward it
Not having a specific, real experience that motivated the shift
keyPoints: Names the real distinction: Analyst works within an existing model; BI Engineer owns the model/pipeline upstream of it
Motivation should come from a specific, real experience, not a vague sense of career progression
Shows concrete action already taken (specific skills being built), not just stated intention
Avoids treating BI Engineering as simply 'more advanced reporting'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the two roles
Gives a specific, credible motivation
Describes concrete action already taken
